notes: The leek, Allium porrum L., known only in cultivation, is a cultigen derived from A. ampeloprasum, which it resembles in flower, but differs in its biennial life-cycle, stout cylindrical bulb, much broader leaves and much less pungent taste. It may survive for a short period as a relic of previous cultivation, and is known as an occasional escape on disturbed sites in metropolitan Perth, Western Australia (Osborne Park, 20 Dec. 1952, collector unknown, PERTH). Variants of A. ampeloprasum with bulbils in the umbel have been recognised in W Europe but are not known to occur in Australia.

Tenth leaf stage: leaves shortly petiolate, apex mucronate, base attenuate, lateral veins not apparent. Cataphylls intermingled with the true leaves. Petioles somewhat decurrent on the stems. Indumentum of dark reddish brown hairs usually visible in the leaf axils.
notes: The flowers are heavily and sweetly perfumed. L.S.Smith (14683) noted that the base of the lower branches is often decumbent and rooting.

Adventive plants have also been sparingly recorded from the Adelaide Hills, South Australia.

distribution_description: Native to South America (southern Brazil, northern Argentina, northeastern Paraguay). In Australia, an escape from cultivation, naturalised in southwestern Western Australia, southeastern Queensland, coastal New South Wales, and sparingly in Victoria; also on Lord Howe and Norfolk Islands.
notes: Occurs as a garden escape that can become an environmental weed. Reported to be naturalised in Dandenong Ranges, southern Victoria, (J.H. Willis, Handb. Pl. Victoria 1: 327, 1970), but no specimens seen. For an account of Alstroemeria psittacina on Norfolk and Lord Howe Islands see Green (1994), as A. pulchella.

habitat_description: The few natural occurrences on Norfolk Island suggest that this species favours streamside and damp forest situations. Can grow in the shade of Norfolk Palm (Rhopalostylis baueri), occasionally on ridges but most commonly in gullies on valley floors or lower valley sides (Director of National Parks 2010: 77).
distribution_description: Endemic to Norfolk Island; now confined to small populations in a few forested valleys.
notes: Achyranthes arborescens, along with A. mangarevica Suess. (from Mangareva Islands, Polynesia) and A. margaretarum de Lange (from Phillip Island), which are not quite as tall, are the only truly arborescent members of the family.

notes: Treatment for Achyranthes aspera L. on Norfolk and Lord Howe Islands provided by Green (1994: 88); for Christmas, Cocos (Keeling) and Coral Sea Islands see Barker & Telford (1993: 115).

distribution_description: Widespread in the drier parts of the tropics and subtropics from western Africa across the Middle East to Burma. It occurs in northern Western Australia in the Kimberley, south to Carnarvon and inland to Wittenoom Gorge; in the Victoria River district and a few other scattered localities in the Northern Territory; Oodnadatta in South Australia; scattered occurrences in north-western Queensland mostly around Cloncurry and further south near Roma; and in the interior of New South Wales.
notes: Aerva javanica is thought to have been accidentally introduced in the 1880s probably in fodder and saddle packs for the Afghan camel trains. Along with Buffel and Birdwood Grasses (Cenchrus spp.) it was later deliberately introduced to the Ord River catchment area in north-western Western Australia to aid in regeneration of overgrazed and water-eroded areas. It has since also proved to be a useful fodder plant for cattle during drought. Being a prolific seeder it has spread across northern Australia by various means, one being as seed contamination of Buffel Grass introductions.

notes: One collection of Gomphrena breviflora (D.H. Perry s.n.), from Ajana near Geraldton in Western Australia is an isolated occurrence quite south of the normal distribution and is probably erroneously labelled.

Also recorded from Timor and the Moluccas.

distribution_description: Widespread and common in the Pilbara and Kimberley regions of Western Australia; in the Northern Territory from Cobourg Peninsula in the north, south to Tennant Creek, across the Barkly Tableland and the Gulf east to Normanton in Queensland. Also extends into Timor and the Moluccas. One collection from Uluru National Park in the south of the Northern Territory is probably the result of an introduction by travellers.

fruiting_time_description: Flowers and fruit all year round

phenology_text: Flowers and fruit all year round.
habitat_description: Gomphrena celosoides is a common weed of disturbed areas, mown lawns and grasslands, mostly in sandy or heavy brown soils.
distribution_description: Native in South America, this species has become a weed in the tropical and subtropical parts of the world including Australia. It occurs in Western Australia at Port Hedland, on the Dampier Peninsula and around Kununurra in the Kimberley; scattered through northern and central Northern Territory and is most widespread in eastern Australia from the islands off Cape York in Queensland to Nowra in southern New South Wales and inland to west of Cunnamulla. It has also been recorded from southern South Australia, and occurs on Christmas Island.
notes: A treatment for Gomphrena celosioides on Christmas Island is provided by Barker in Barker & Telford (1993: 118). Horses may be poisoned if confined to areas with large amounts of this species but little other fodder, suffering from ‘Coastal Staggers’ (Everist 1974: 57).

distribution_description: Occurs in Queensland on Cape York Peninsula, from Goode Island in the north along the coastline including several offshore islands and inland to near the Laura River west of Cooktown.
notes: Bentham (1870) cites a specimen collected by Bynoe of this species from the Victoria River in the Northern Territory (K 000357258). This specimen is Gomphrena conferta but as there are no other collections from this area, the occurrence of this species in the Northern Territory requires confirming.

Distribution in Australia is scattered: Broome and Kununurra in Western Australia, southern Northern Territory, Renmark, South Australia, and from near Rockhampton in south-eastern Queensland to just S of Newcastle and W of Tamworth, New South Wales.
notes: This species seems to be moving around Australia, especially down the eastern coastline, probably by way of tourist traffic.

Normanby River, V.J. Neldner 3821 (DNA)' determined as Pupalia micrantha - Editor.]

ecology_description: The flowers open in the evening and are pollinated by a hawk moth, recorded by H.N. Ridley (loc. cit.), as Sphinx convolvuli (Agrius convolvuli (Linnaeus 1758)) on Christmas Island. The erect inflorescences often deposit their seed higher up the cliff than the parent plant, leading to a slow ascent up the cliffs. The inland cliffs on Christmas Island must have been first colonised when they were at sea level, and have maintained their populations since.
habitat_description: H.N. Ridley, Journal of the Straits Branch of the Royal Asiatic Society 45: 236 (1906), recorded it as common on Christmas Island in Flying Fish Cove and on rocks and cliffs throughout. It has been removed from most readily accessible situations for cultivation in gardens but is still quite frequent on exposed cliffs, both at the coast and on the tiers of inland cliffs. It grows in partially shady to very exposed situations, on ledges and in crevices in the limestone. On Cocos (Keeling) Islands grows in coralline sand at the top of beaches, or in gullies or depressions.
distribution_description: Occurs on Christmas Island and Cocos (Keeling) Islands. A widespread species, distributed from Sri Lanka and India to S China and Japan, through Indo-China, Malesia, the Philippines to the Pacific islands.

distribution_description: Native in coastal swamps and on river banks, on Wessel Is., N.T., along the coast and offshore islands in Qld and in N.S.W. south to Jervis Bay. Also on Norfolk and Lord Howe Islands, and in New Guinea. J.G. Baker (Handbook of the Amaryllideae 77, 1888) recorded it for New Caledonia, Fiji and Timor.
notes: Characterised by the robust pseudostem, large broad leaves with entire margins, large inflorescence arising in leaf axil and pedicellate flowers with narrow decurving perianth lobes and long straight anthers. Although the name Crinum asiaticum L. has been misapplied to C. angustifolium in Australia, C. asiaticum appears to be more closely related to C. pedunculatum. The delimitation between these two species needs further investigation. Particular attention should be paid to ovule number. For treatment of Crinum pedunculatum on Norfolk and Lord Howe Islands see Green (1994: 509--510), as Crinum asiaticum L. var. pedunculatum (R.Br.) Fosberg & Sachet.

ecology_description: There is a record of a large number of seedlings in partial to deep shade beneath Alstonia scholaris, Acacia and Corymbia sp. where the nearest adult plant is unknown but it is thought to have been dispersed to the site by rats or cockatoos (viz. B.M. Waterhouse 6846; BRI). Also possibly dispersed by fruit bats (viz. B.M. Waterhouse 4285; BRI, MEL). Has potential to become a serious environmental weed locally, e.g. on Horn Island where seedlings and saplings are clustered and often abundant beneath trees which provide perching or roosting sites for fruit bats and cockatoos (viz. B.M. Waterhouse 2999, 5339; BRI). Pollination biology of cashew, including insects visiting the flowers, has been investigated in the Northern Territory; see Heard et al. (1990).

ecology_description: Widespread in northern Australia with most occurrences a result from human activities but the seeds are also spread by other vectors. The fallen fruit is eaten by cattle, and horses will spit the seeds out. Fruiting attracts Fruit Bats/Flying Foxes (Pteropus spp.). (Zich et al. 2018). The disseminule has been recorded as flotsam on Ashmore Reef islands, and is described and illustrated by Pike & Leach (1997: 126, 138). A diversity of insects visit mango flowers, including many species of bees, wasps, flies, beetles, ants and butterflies. Studies suggest that flies are important in mango pollination. As pollinators for economic crops such as mangos, flies are likely to represent a good alternative or supplemental option to bees because different species are present all year round and frequently visit flowers to feed on nectar and/or pollen to support key biological functions including flight and reproduction. (Cook et al. 2020); see Cook et al. (2020), and references therein, for details.

It is now quite common on the island, and many specimens are self-sown. The natural distribution of Mangifera ×odorata has been obscured through its widespread cultivation throughout Malesia, but it occurs in lowland forest in Sumatra, Java and Borneo.
notes: A second species of mango, Mangifera indica L., is also cultivated on Christmas Island. This species is probably native to India and Burma, but is widely cultivated throughout the tropics, and is commercially the most important mango. The seed produced on Christmas Island is viable and seedlings will grow freely if the fruit is not collected, suggesting that this species may become naturalised in the future. The fruit is delicious eaten raw or dried, and may be used to make pickles, chutney or jam. It is most easily distinguished from M. ×odorata by its more slender, glossy leaves with an undulating margin, its shortly hairy inflorescence, its broader, papillose disc and its more brightly coloured fruit; D.A. notes: This species shows strong heterophylly, with remarkable variation in size, form and pigmentation of leaf laminas. The corolla lobes show variation in pubescence: plants with the distal portion of the lobes glabrous have been distinguished as var. glabrata by some earlier authors, but this variety is not maintained here as there appears to be no correlation of this feature with other characters.

notes: Parsonsia velutina has the widest range in Australia of any Parsonsia and shows marked variation in leaf size, indumentum and inflorescence morphology. The variation is in part geographical and may, with further study, allow recognition or reinstatement of two or more distinct taxa. The species, as here circumscribed, is distinguished by the usually medium-sized to large, ovate or oblong-ovate leaves, the usual presence of a dense, soft, fawn to brown tomentum on the laminas, and the consistently cordate lamina base, by the small flowers that are subsessile and in dense, discrete clusters within the panicle, by the corolla with erect lobes which enclose the anther cone, and by the spreading sepals. Populations from New South Wales and southern Queensland have short peduncles 0.2--3 cm long, while the northern Australian specimens have much longer peduncles to 13 cm long, and usually have the bifurcation or trifurcation at the peduncle apex well-developed. The leaf indumentum shows much variation. Within one region different populations may be softly fawn-pubescent, densely rusty-pubescent or glabrescent to almost glabrous.

distribution_description: Natural occurrence unclear, but probably Indochina to Malesia, southern Japan and northern Australia, now pantropical and pansubtropical in cultivation as the staple starch crop Taro. notes: Contains an irritant sap (Du Puy 1993: 439). For an account of Colocasia esculenta occurring on Christmas Island, where it was introduced by the Chinese and found in gardens and on the fringes of many cultivated areas and around habitation, see Du Puy (1993: 439). For an account of Colocasia esculenta occurring on Norfolk and Lord Howe Islands see Du Puy (1994: 416--417).

leaf_description: Leaves | petiole to c. 1 m long (usually less), apically geniculate, sheathing in lower c. 1/2--2/3 | wings of sheath persistent except for scarious extreme margin | blade entire, lanceolate and sometimes grey-variegated when juvenile, becoming (elliptic to) oblong-ovate to broadly ovate, to c. 1 m long | venation differentiated into numerous primary veins alternating with less robust parallel secondary veins
inflorescence_description: Inflorescence solitary, rarely paired, c. 20 cm long | spathe green outside, dirty cream within, marcescent and blackening | spadix subsessile, thick, bluntly spindle shaped, slightly shorter than spathe
flower_description: Stigmas slit-like to broadly punctate (often mixed shapes in one spadix), sessile
fruit_description: Infructescence orange | the fruits dehiscent
habitat_description: Grows inpermanently or almost permanently swampy sites or near permanent springs at lowelevation.
distribution_description: Occurs from New Guinea, the Bismarck Archipelago to Vanuatu; in Australia from scattered tropical localities in Qld and the N.T.
notes: Most easily confused with Rhaphidophora australasica which is smaller, with the leaf sheath degrading to fibres, and the stigmas raised and finely punctate. Epipremnum amplissimum differs from Scindapsus altissimus (with which it can easily be confused at first sight) in the somewhat bluish leaves, flowering on adherent shoots with internodes up to c. twice as long as thick where S. altissimus has deep green somewhat glossy leaves, adherent shoots with internodes several times longer than wide, and flowering on free lateral shoots; the inflorescences of S. altissimus are longer and thinner than those of E. amplissimum. Juveniles of E. amplissimum may form extensive swards in open swampy areas, and are often but not always bluish grey-variegated.

flowering_time_description: Flowers recorded Sept.-Nov., but few fertile collections and probably flowering longer
habit_description: Robust bole climber, feeder roots corky
leaf_description: Leaves | petiole to c. 70 cm long, sheathing for most of length, apically geniculate | sheath degrading to copious fibres | blade simple, oblong-ovate, entire in juveniles gradually becoming increasingly pinnatifid by fenestration in adult plants, rarely entire in adult plants, often with pin-prick holes near midrib, to c. 70 cm long, with up to c. 12 segments per side of midrib | segments (except apical and basal compound segments) each with 1 primary vein, obliquely truncate at apex | secondary venation reticulate
inflorescence_description: Inflorescences usually multiple, in an apical cluster | subtending bracts degrading like leaf sheath into multiple papery fibres | spathe c. 20 cm long, thick, greenish outside, dirty cream inside, opening boat-shaped, caducous | spadix subsessile, slightly shorter than spathe
flower_description: Stigmas slit-like
fruit_description: Infructescence green, with distal parts of ovary shed in coherent plates revealing orange pulp
phenology_text: Flowers recorded Sept.-Nov., but few fertile collections and probably flowering longer.
habitat_description: Generally occurring in regrowth, forest margin or gallery forest; sea level to c. 350 m alt.
distribution_description: Widespread through Indomalesia and into Oceania; in Australia known from warmer lowland and lower montane rainforest and monsoon forest areas of E Qld, from Torres Str. to Ingham, with disjunct records to Rockhampton and as far S as Noosa Natl Park (but possibly cultivated there).
notes: Juvenile plants with entire leaves are easily recognised by their reticulate leaf venation and longitudinal crests in the internodes.

flowering_time_description: Flowers year round, thoughmay stagnate in winter in cooler areas
habit_description: Evergreen geophytic herb
underground_organ_description: rhizome condensed, creeping, bearing thick subtuberous roots
leaf_description: Leaves very tough, few to several together, distichous, not differentiated into petiole and blade, linear, conduplicate, to c. 1.5 m long, mostly 1--1.5 cm wide | margin and midrib somewhat and finely erose-dentate | venation parallel to midrib | usually 1 thick tough primary vein on each side and 1 or more of lesser thickness
inflorescence_description: Inflorescence compound, an alate peduncle to c. 3 m tall bearing distant flattened bracts, the upper ones with 1 or more sessile or shortly stalked spikelet-like synflorescences in its axil | synflorescence perennial, a condensed sympodium consisting of repeated units composed of prophyll, cataphyll and spadix, each unit arising in axil of previous cataphyll | spathe absent | spadices often in several stages of maturity at once in each synflorescence, stipitate, at first with flowers crowded, later elongating and by male anthesis the flowers somewhat distant
flower_description: Flowers bisexual, tetramerous, tepalate, greenish, later becoming dark brown | Stamens with flattened filaments | Ovary unilocular, uniovulate with apical placentation
fruit_description: Fruit an ovoid blue-black berry
phenology_text: Flowers year round, thoughmay stagnate in winter in cooler areas.
habitat_description: Grows in warm temperate, subtropical and tropical rainforest, submontane rainforest and wet sclerophyll forests.
distribution_description: Queensland from near Cape Tribulation to the New South Wales south coast, from sea level to over 1000 m alt.

underground_organ_description: Roots (1-) 2--7 (-12), to 7 cm long, all perforating the scale
leaf_description: Fronds obovate, 1.5--8 mm long, 1.5--2 times as long as wide, pointed at apex, flat or gibbous, without red spot on upper surface | nerves 3--7
flower_description: Flowers 1- or 2-ovulate
fruit_description: Fruit 0.8--1.0 mm long, with lateral wings towards top
seed_description: Seeds with 10--15 distinct ribs
habitat_description: Grows in eutrophic, quiet waters in suboceanic, temperate to subtropical regions.
distribution_description: Occurs in W.A., S.A., Qld, N.S.W., Vic. and Tas. Originally from south-east Asia, Australia and the Pacific Islands; introduced into many parts of the world.

flowering_time_description: Flowers and fruits throughout the year
fruiting_time_description: Flowers and fruits throughout the year
underground_organ_description: Roots to 3 cm long | sheath winged at base | tip usually sharply pointed
leaf_description: Fronds floating on water surface, ovate to lanceolate, with obtuse to shortly pointed tip, 1--6 mm long, 1--3 times as long as wide, flat, entire, with distinct papule near tip and above node, without red colour, without a green stalk | nerves 3 | air spaces in 2 or 3 layers spreading through most of frond, shorter than 0.3 mm
flower_description: Flowers 1-ovulate
fruit_description: Fruit 0.5--0.8 mm long, not winged
seed_description: Seeds with 9--26 distinct ribs
phenology_text: Flowers and fruits throughout the year.
habitat_description: Mesotrophic to eutrophic; grows in quiet waters.
distribution_description: Found in tropical to warm temperate zones throughout the world. Occurs in W.A., N.T., Qld and N.S.W.

flowering_time_description: Flowers and fruits (rarely) throughout the year
fruiting_time_description: Flowers and fruits (rarely) throughout the year
underground_organ_description: Roots to 15 cm long | sheath not winged | tip usually rounded
leaf_description: Fronds floating on water surface, obovate, with obtuse to shortly pointed tip, 0.8--4 mm long, 1--2 times as long as wide, flat or gibbous, entire, with distinct papule near apex and above node, sometimes red on lower surface, especially near margins, occasionally with distinct reddish spots on upper surface, without green stalk | nerves 3--5 | the lateral nerves originating from node, air spaces in 2 or 3 layers spreading through most of frond, with largest ones mostly longer than 0.3 mm
flower_description: Flowers 1 or 2 (-3)-ovulate
fruit_description: Fruit 0.7--0.8 mm long, with lateral wings towards top
seed_description: Seeds with 10--16 distinct ribs
phenology_text: Flowers and fruits (rarely) throughout the year.
habitat_description: Grows in eutrophic, quiet waters in suboceanic temperate regions.
distribution_description: Occurs in W.A., S.A., N.S.W., A.C.T., Vic. and Tas. Also found in New Zealand.

underground_organ_description: Roots to 15 cm long | sheath not winged | tip usually rounded
leaf_description: Fronds floating on water surface, obovate, with obtuse to shortly pointed tip, 1--8 mm long, 1.3--2 times as long as wide, flat, entire, with an indistinct papule near apex and above node, sometimes diffusely red coloured on upper surface, but not on lower surface, without green stalk | nerves 3--5 (if more than 3 nerves then outer ones branching from base of inner ones) | air spaces in 2 or 3 layers spreading through most of frond, shorter than 0.3 mm
flower_description: Flowers 1-ovulate
fruit_description: Fruit 0.8--1.0 mm long, with lateral wings towards top
seed_description: Seeds with 8--15 distinct ribs
habitat_description: Mesotrophic to eutrophic; grows in quiet waters in suboceanic, cool temperate regions.
distribution_description: Introduced into Vic., in the vicinity of Melbourne. Originally distributed through Eurasia, Africa and N America.

underground_organ_description: Roots to 2.5 cm long | sheath not winged | tip sharply pointed
leaf_description: Fronds submerged or (when flowering) floating on water surface, lanceolate, tapering to long pointed tip, 3.5--9 mm long, 2.5--4 times (flowering fronds 1--2 times) as long as wide, flat, entire, without papules and red colour, without a green stalk | nerves 3 | air spaces in 1 layer spreading through less than 1/2 frond (throughout most of frond in flowering fronds), shorter than 0.3 mm
flower_description: Flowers 1-ovulate
fruit_description: Fruit not known
phenology_text: Flowering (very rare); probably throughout the year.
habitat_description: Grows in Melaleuca swamps; mesotrophic, found in quiet water in tropical regions.
distribution_description: In Australia, occurs in northern N.T.; also in Malaysia, Burma and Vietnam, and has been recorded from Singapore but is now extinct.
notes: Records of L. trisulca from the Kimberley region, W.A., and Qld might be misidentifications of this species.

underground_organ_description: Roots to 2.5 cm long (in Australian plants often not developed) | sheath not winged | tip sharply pointed
leaf_description: Fronds submerged (flowering fronds floating on water surface), very often forming branched chains, narrowly ovate, with obtuse to shortly pointed tip, narrowed at base into a 2--20 mm long green stalk, 3--15 mm long (without stalk), 2--3.5 times as long as wide, flat, with denticulate margins in distal part, without papules, at most slightly reddish | nerves 1 or 3 | air spaces in 1 or 2 layers, only in distal part of frond, shorter than 0.3 mm
flower_description: Flowers 1-ovulate
fruit_description: Fruit 0.6--0.9 mm long, with lateral wings towards top
seed_description: Seeds with 12--18 distinct ribs
habitat_description: Mesotrophic; grows in quiet waters in cool temperate regions.
distribution_description: Occurs in S.A., Qld, N.S.W., A.C.T., Vic. and Tas. Reports from W.A. (Kimberley region) and N.T. are probably erroneous. Also found in Eurasia, Africa and N America.

common_name: Fruit Salad Plant, Swiss Cheese Plant.
habit_description: See Spencer (2005; 15), Richardson et al. (2025; 15)
distribution_description: Native of Central America. Sparingly naturalised in N.S.W.

habit_description: Floating mat-forming stoloniferous aquatic
leaf_description: leaves shortly petiolate, suboblong, hairy, inflated, in a lettuce-like rosette to c. 30 cm diam
inflorescence_description: Inflorescence mostly solitary, physiognomically axillary, inconspicuous at leaf bases, c. 1 cm long | spathe hairy outside, slightly constricted | limb subcampanulate, white inside | spadix shorter than spathe | female zone a solitary naked pistil adnate to spathe | male zone a stipitate ring of anthers subtended by a membranous collar | appendix absent
fruit_description: Fruit a multi-seeded inconspicuous greenish berry
vegetative_reproduction_description: The plants can reproduce vegetatively with great rapidity and may become noxious weeds
habitat_description: Found in permanent still to slow-moving water having high nutrient levels.
distribution_description: Pantropical. In Australia in scattered tropical localities in N.T. and Qld. S.L.W.Jacobs (pers. comm.) regarded it as probably, though uncertainly, native in N.T. in areas of natural high nutrient levels such as Arafura Swamp. J.D.Gillett, Australian Weeds Research Newsletter 37: 91 (1988), noted that P. stratiotes had been recorded in an unspecified ‘remote locality’ in N.T. in 1887. Elsewhere in the tropics, it appears generally to be associated with water whose nutrient levels have been elevated by agricultural activities, and should perhaps be regarded there as naturalised; in cooler areas, it occurs occasionally as an escape from ornamental horticulture in ponds and aquaria.
notes: Inflorescence structure is considerably modified from that of other aroids and its development has been described and illustrated in detail recently by Buzgo, Bot. Jahrb. Syst. 115: 557--570 (1994). According to Sainty & Jacobs, Waterpl. New South Wales 66 (1981), seeds are not recorded in Australia. The plants can reproduce vegetatively with great rapidity and may become noxious weeds.

peduncle_length_description: peduncle, oblong-ovoid, to c. 2 cm long
habit_description: Slender hemi-epiphytic rainforest and gallery forest climber on tree boles and rocks
leaf_description: Leaves | petiole shorter than blade, sheathing for most of length, apically geniculate with sheath not quite reaching geniculum | wings of sheath membranous, persistent, eventually becoming fibrous | blade elliptic, slightly to distinctly falcate, c. 12 × 5 cm, acute to obtuse and minutely auriculate at base, dull mid green
inflorescence_description: Inflorescence solitary or paired, terminal on leafy ultimate branchlets | spathe reflexed, broadly ovate, c. 2 cm long, mucronate for c. 3 mm, green | spadix sessile, with base of spathe margins somewhat decurrent on peduncle, oblong-ovoid, to c. 2 cm long, ivory-white
habitat_description: Grows in rainforest fromthe lowlands to c. 1200 m alt.
distribution_description: Endemic to NE Qld between Daintree and Bellenden Ker.

habit_description: Slender climber or hemi-epiphyte with well differentiated adherent climbing shoots and free lateral flowering branches
leaf_description: Leaves | petiole usually exceeding blade in length | lamina-like, oblanceolate, 2--12 cm × 4--14 mm, distally obtuse to truncate to strongly auriculate | blade elliptic to narrowly lanceolate, 1.5--15 cm long, 3--15 mm wide, rounded at base, somewhat acuminate, glossy dark green above
inflorescence_description: Inflorescence solitary or paired, in axils mostly of distal leaves of flowering branches and subtended by cataphylls | peduncle 2--5 cm long | spadix yellow to purplish, to c. 6 cm long, sessile or more usually distinctly stipitate | spathe lanceolate, c. 1.5--4 × 0.5--0.9 cm, wide-opening to reflexed, purple-black to greenish
habitat_description: Grows in rainforests at low altitudes in cooler parts of range, extending to c. 1000 m alt. further north.
distribution_description: Occurs in eastern Australia from northern Qld to north-eastern N.S.W.

habit_description: Lithophytic herb
underground_organ_description: corm subhemispherical, to c. 5 cm diam. | stolons erect, unbranched, to c. 30 cm long, bearing numerous clusters of ovoid hooked bulbils
leaf_description: Leaves 1-several together | petiole to c. 50 cm long, sheathing in lower c. ¼ | blade broadly ovatosagittate, peltate, shining bright green, pendent, to c. 40 cm long, secondary venation not forming interprimary collective veins
inflorescence_description: Inflorescence seldom found (in Australia), mostly solitary or 2 together in series, produced before leaves | spathe c. 11 cm long, constricted, lower spathe narrowly ovoid, green, spathe limb broadly spathulate, yellow | spadix reaching c. 1/2 length of spathe limb | male zone clavate
habitat_description: Lithophytic in rainforest, or terrestrial among boulders, near creek beds or on forest floor, often in sandy soils.
distribution_description: Widely distributed from seasonal areas from W tropical Africa to Taiwan and Australia; so far as is known absent from Malesia except Java; in Australia known only from a few localities in N.T., tropical Qld and from Christmas Is.
notes: Flowering appears to be uncommon through much of the range of this species.

habit_description: Moderately robust bole-climber, occasionally scrambling over rocks, to c. 30 m tall, without free lateral shoots
leaf_description: Leaves | petiole generally somewhat shorter than blade, sheathing to geniculum | sheath degrading to papery fibres then falling away altogether | blade oblanceolate-elliptic, slightly falcate, to c. 40 cm long × c. 14 cm wide, glossy green above, dull below, somewhat coriaceous, primary venation not strongly differentiated from secondary
inflorescence_description: Inflorescences solitary or 2 together, smelling of decomposing plant matter | spathe c. (6-) 10--15 cm long, cream to greenish cream | spadix c. ½-¾ length of spathe, sessile to shortly stipitate | Fruiting spadix to c. 11 cm long, orange after dehiscence
flower_description: Ovary topped with conic style to c. 0.6 mm long | stigma punctate to transversely shortly linear
habitat_description: Found in areas supporting lowland and lower montane rainforest, in forest and regrowth, from sea level to c. 1000 m alt.
distribution_description: Endemic in NE Qld, between c. Ingham and Cooktown.

habit_description: Slender bole climber to c. 20 m tall
stem_description: stems adherent, often spiralling up substrate, sometimes producing much reduced, condensed detachable short-shoots and elongate flagelliform foraging shoots with reduced leaf blades
leaf_description: Leaves appressed to substrate | petiole much shorter than blade, c. 1.5 cm long, sheathing throughout and wings of sheath with paperymembranous ligulate extensions along stem to c. half length of blade | blade broadly ovate, to c. 15 cm long, shallowly cordate at base, velvety dark grey-green adaxially, paler abaxially, coriaceous
inflorescence_description: Inflorescence | spathe c. 6 cm long | spadix shortly stipitate, subcylindric (spindle-shaped), c. 4.5 cm long
flower_description: Stigmas sessile, mostly punctate, slit-like in lower flowers
habitat_description: Grows in lowland rainforest and complex mesophyll vine forest to c. 400 m alt.
distribution_description: Endemic to NE Qld, from S of Cooktown to Innisfail.
notes: The shingle-leaf habit of this species is found in the juvenile phases of several Malesian species of Rhaphidophora (e.g. R. korthalsii Schott) which suggests that this species flowers while persistently juvenile - an example of neoteny.

habit_description: Moderately robust bole-climber or hemi-epiphyte to c. 20 m tall, clinging axes monopodial, producing free lateral sympodial flowering shoots
leaf_description: Leaves | sheath degrading to papery fibres then falling altogether | blade narrowly ovate to lanceolate, somewhat falcate, to c. 18 cm × 6 cm (somewhat larger on clinging axes), dull mid green above, paler below, rather thinly coriaceous
inflorescence_description: Inflorescence solitary on a short stout ascending peduncle | spathe broadly ovate, cowl-like, c. 8 cm long, thick, creamy yellow | spadix stipitate for c. 1 cm, with fertile part c. 6 × 2 cm, bluntly tapering
flower_description: Ovary obpyramidal, bearing a punctate stigma on a style c. 0.6 mm long
habitat_description: Found in areas supporting lowland to lower montane rainforest, in forest and regrowth, from sea level to c. 800 m.
distribution_description: Endemic in NE Qld, between Innisfail and Daintree.

habit_description: Immense climber or sprawling lithophyte to c. 60 m tall
leaf_description: Leaves | petiole to c. 80 cm long, sheathing for most of length | wings of sheath persistent | blade oblong-ovate, to c. 80 cm long, entire, shining dark green | venation not or hardly differentiated into primary or secondary veins | densely striate
inflorescence_description: Inflorescence cylindric, c. 30 cm long | spathe green to yellowish, opening narrowly canoe-shaped, caducous | spadix subsessile, narrowly cylindric, slightly shorter than spathe, green
fruit_description: Fruits transversely dehiscent in coherent plates revealing red pulp
phenology_text: Flowers June-Oct. (based on a small sample).
habitat_description: Grows inrainforest, riparian and gallery forest, evergreen notophyll vine forest, climbing on trees or sprawling on rocks, from sea level to c. 400 m alt.
distribution_description: In NE Qld on Cape York Penin., from Iron Ra. to McIlwraith Ra.; also in New Guinea. Its occurrence at Bamaga, reported by A.Hay (Telopea 5: 299 (1993)), was based on misidentification with Epipremnum amplissimum.

underground_organ_description: Roots 7--21, to 3 cm long, with 1 or 2 perforating the scale
leaf_description: Fronds obovate to circular, 2--10 mm long, 1--1.5 times as long as wide, rounded or pointed at apex, flat or rarely slightly gibbous, sometimes with red spot in centre of upper surface | nerves 7--16 (-21)
flower_description: disc-shaped to reniform, 1--2 mm diam., brownish to olive | Flowers (very rare) 1- or 2-ovulate
fruit_description: Fruit 1.0--1.5 mm long, with lateral wings towards top
seed_description: Seeds with 12--20 distinct ribs
habitat_description: Grows in eutrophic, quiet waters.
distribution_description: Almost worldwide distribution in temperate to tropical regions; in S America only in the north; in Australia occurs in N.T., Qld, N.S.W. and Vic.

habit_description: Cormous to rhizomatous herb
underground_organ_description: corm subglobose, to c. 5 cm diam. or rhizome tuberous, creeping, c. 2--3 cm diam
leaf_description: Leaves several together | petiole c. 20--40 cm long, sheathing in lower 1/4--3/4 | blades variable in size and shape, oblong-elliptic with base obtuse, to hastate to deeply trifid with linear lobes, anterior lobe c. 10--35 cm long, posterior lobes lacking to c. 6 cm long, distinctly shorter than anterior lobe
inflorescence_description: Inflorescence | spathe to c. 25 cm long, constricted c. 4 cm from base | limb narrowly to broadly ovate, spreading, then gradually tapering and acuminate, brownish purple | spadix generally subequalling spathe, occasionally reaching only c. 1/2 way along limb | female zone 0.5--1 cm long, then a c. 0.5 cm long zone of crowded filiform neuter organs, then a naked interstice c. 2 cm long | male zone c. 2 cm long | appendix narrowly conic, to 14 cm long, usually shortly to conspicuously stipitate, with base usually obtuse (to truncate)
fruit_description: Infructescence within persistent spathe base
dispersal_description: The current circumscription of this species, covering a large fragmented range, wide climatic amplitude and considerable morphological variation represented by scant, often poor herbarium material, should be regarded as no more than provisional
vegetative_reproduction_description: Collections from this area of S.A. also have rhizomatous rather than cormous stems, and, with the short, truncate-based appendix, thus link this ‘species’ with T. brownii, though the leaves, with reduced posterior lobes, nevertheless remain distinctive
habitat_description: Little data is available on habitats through the range, though in S.A., it is recorded growing in braids of deep heavy soil in rocky, gypseous, seasonally dry creek beds, lined with ‘Eucalyptus coolabah’ and Acacia cambagei, in gibber landscape.
distribution_description: N.T., Qld, S.A.; from Cape York Penin. to Central Australia.
notes: Recent collections from S.A.are new generic records for that state. The current circumscription of this species, covering a large fragmented range, wide climatic amplitude and considerable morphological variation represented by scant, often poor herbarium material, should be regarded as no more than provisional. Further field studies are required. Hay (loc. cit.) noted some apparent intermediates with T. angustilobum. Bates 47101 (AD) has the appendix truncate at base and reaching only c. halfway along the spathe limb. Collections from this area of S.A. also have rhizomatous rather than cormous stems, and, with the short, truncate-based appendix, thus link this ‘species’ with T. brownii, though the leaves, with reduced posterior lobes, nevertheless remain distinctive. Moreover, these plants are ecologically very distinct from T. brownii. Symon 15681 (NSW) is extraordinarily robust, with leaf blades c. 35 × 13 cm.

habit_description: Cormous herb
underground_organ_description: corm subglobose to irregular and flattish, 4--10 cm wide
leaf_description: Leaves few to several together | petiole to 35 cm long | blade slightly glaucous, very variable in shape, hastate to deeply trifid with linear lobes, anterior lobe c. 16--19 cm long, 0.5--9 cm wide, posterior lobes about ¾ length of anterior, tending to be held above plane of anterior lobe
inflorescence_description: Inflorescence | peduncle short | spathe to c. 22 cm long, constricted c. 3--5 cm from base | limb very broadly ovate, somewhat convolute basally, purplish brown inside, greenish outside | spadix (often much) shorter than spathe, c. 6--11 cm long | female zone c. 0.8 cm long, then a 0.5 cm zone of crowded filiform neuter organs, then a naked interstice c. 2 cm long | male zone 0.8--2 cm long | appendix variable in size and shape, stipitate, broadly conical and oblique-truncate at base, 2--6 cm long, purple-black
fruit_description: Infructescence within persistent spathe base
distribution_description: Found in northern Qld, extending to Southern New Guinea, in open woodland.

habit_description: Small evergreen herb
underground_organ_description: rhizome tuberous, c. 2 cm diam., ovoid to spindleshaped, bearing several small, easily detached ovoid cormels
leaf_description: Leaves several together | petioles to c. 20 cm long, shortly sheathing | blades sagittate, c. 12 × 5 cm, deep bright green, membranous
inflorescence_description: Inflorescence among leaves, sometimes several in succession | peduncle much shorter than petioles | spathe to c. 20 cm long, lower spathe convolute, elliptic, to 3 cm long, greenish brown outside, spathe limb spreading, to c. 18 cm long, broadly ovate below, then long-acuminate, the distal portion often twisted, glistening velvety purple inside, greenish brown outside | spadix c. equalling spathe | female zone c. 0.8 cm long, then a 1 cm zone of crowded sinuous filiform neuter organs, then a naked interstice c. 2 cm long | male zone to 1.2 cm long | appendix slender and tapering, faintly swollen at oblique base, to c. 15 cm long, rough to verruculose, purple-black
flower_description: anthers with shortly beaked connective
fruit_description: Infructescence within persistent spathe base
phenology_text: Floweringtime expected to be throughout all but the driest periods.
vegetative_reproduction_description: Propagation appears to be vegetative through the production of copious cormels
distribution_description: Virtually pantropical. Nicolson & Sivadasan, loc. cit. concluded that this species is native to China and Japan. In Australia it has recently been found naturalised in N Qld.
notes: Propagation appears to be vegetative through the production of copious cormels.

habit_description: Rhizomatous herb, tending to form colonies
underground_organ_description: rhizome to c. 15 cm long, c. 2--3 cm diam., creeping and proliferating through production of tubercles
leaf_description: Leaves several together | petiole 10--25 (-70) cm long | blade deeply hastate to ternatifid, rarely with lobes almost linear, paleish mid green, membranous, anterior lobe to c. 20 × 12 cm, posterior lobes c. 1/2 length of anterior
inflorescence_description: Inflorescences with and subtended by leaves, solitary to several in succession interspersed by leaves | spathe to 20 cm long, lower spathe c. 4 cm long, broadly globosecylindric, separated from limb by an abrupt constriction | limb broadly ovate, spreading, acuminate, deep purple inside, greenish outside | spadix markedly shorter than spathe | female zone 1--2 cm long, then a zone c. 0.5 cm long of crowded filiform neuter organs, then a naked zone c. 3 cm long (sometimes with a few papillae immediately below male zone) | male zone 1--1.5 cm long | appendix conical, to c. 5 cm long, obliquely truncate at base, blackish purple
fruit_description: Infructescence within persistent spathe base
habitat_description: Grows in or near areas supporting rainforest or wet sclerophyll forest, in creek banksand often near waterfalls in spray zone.
distribution_description: Occurs from central E Qld to central coastal N.S.W.
notes: A population, apparently of or allied to this species, found c. 21 km W of Glenreagh (N.S.W., North Coast) on Black Range Rd, differs markedly in leaf colour (mid blue-green, with whitish venation) and texture (somewhat thicker), but is not yet known in flower (S.Clemesha, pers. comm.). It warrants further investigation.

habit_description: Cormous herb
leaf_description: Leaves several | petiole c. 11 cm long, sheathing in lower 1/3--1/2 | blade very variable in shape, elliptic with an obtuse base, to hastate to very deeply and narrowly trilobed, to c. 12 cm long, posterior lobes, when present, up to c. 1/2 length of anterior
inflorescence_description: Inflorescence | peduncle mostly subterranean | spathe c. 17 cm long, lower spathe c. 1.5 cm long, ovoid-cylindric, separated from limb by an abrupt constriction, minutely hairy internally | limb ovate, long-acuminate, spreading below, twisted above, brown-purple | spadix somewhat exceeding spathe, to 22 cm long | female zone c. 0.5 cm long, then a 0.5 cm zone of very fine and crowded filiform neuter organs, then a c. 2 cm naked interstice | male zone c. 1.5 cm long | appendix very slender and attenuate, vermiform, but base expanded into an oblique cap like the bowl of a spoon inverted over a short stipe
fruit_description: Infructescence within persistent spathe base
distribution_description: N.T. from Darwin to Arnhemland, mostly in open forest.

flowering_time_description: Flowers mainly Oct., extending to Dec., with one collection in June.
habit_description: Rhizomatous herb
underground_organ_description: rhizome tuberous, creeping, to c. 12 cm long, c. 2 cm diam
leaf_description: Leaves several together | petiole to c. 40 cm long, sheathing in lower 1/3--2/3 | blade hastate to deeply trifid with linear lobes, anterior lobe c. 10--20 × 2--8 cm, posterior lobes to c. 13 × 1.5--5 cm
inflorescence_description: Inflorescence among leaves | spathe to c. 22 cm long, lower spathe ovoid, separated from limb by a rather weak constriction | limb lanceolate, canoe-shaped, attenuate, purplish brown inside, greenish outside | spadix equalling spathe | female zone c. 1 cm long | sterile interstice 2--4 cm long with filiform neuter organs near female zone and more sparsely distributed shorter neuter organs extending up to male zone | male zone c. 1--1.5 × 0.7 cm | appendix sessile, narrowly tapering, c. 7--14 cm long, purplish black
fruit_description: Infructescence within persistent spathe base
phenology_text: Flowers mainly Oct., extending to Dec., with one collection in June.
habitat_description: Grows in damp places in or on the edge of rainforest or in creek banks.
distribution_description: Occurs in coastal N.S.W. from near Myall Lakes to Batemans Bay.

underground_organ_description: Rhizome cormous, stoloniferous, c. 2 cm diam
leaf_description: Leaves several together, appearing before inflorescence | petiole c. 10--30 cm long | blade elliptic to ovate, c. 6--25 cm long, with base acute to auriculate to cordate to hastate, pale to mid green
inflorescence_description: Inflorescence with short peduncle, rarely lifting inflorescence away from leaf bases | spathe base longitudinally keeled, to c. 3.5 cm long, greenish white to pinkish | limb narrowly lanceolate, sometimes long-acuminate, 10--25 cm long, proximally spreading, distally recurved or coiled, purplish brown to white inside, greenish outside | spadix equalling spathe | female zone c. 5 mm long | sterile interstice c. 2 cm long, bearing spreading distant black- or purple-tipped neuter organs c. 6 mm long in lower 1/2, narrowly pyramidal to filiform neuter organs c. 3 mm long in upper 1/2 | male zone c. 5 mm long | appendix subsessile, to c. 20 cm long, usually tapering from base, rarely stouter about 1/3 along its length, deeply ridged and channelled, yellowish green
flower_description: anthers yellow with beaked connective
fruit_description: Infructescence within persistent spathe base, first
habitat_description: Ecological amplitude is wide, from the undergrowth ofswampy forest to open monsoonal savannah and eucalypt woodland, at lowelevation.
distribution_description: Found from Sri Lanka to Indochina, S Malesia, northern Philippines, southern New Guinea and northern Australia (Top End of N.T. and Cape York Penin., Qld).

underground_organ_description: Corm hemispheric, c. 1.5 cm diam., cream
leaf_description: Leaves 5 together | petiole 4 cm long, sheathing in lower 3.5 cm | blade elliptic, c. 3.5 cm long × 1.7 cm wide, obtuse at base, shortly apiculate, dull light green, somewhat coriaceous
inflorescence_description: Inflorescence arising among leaves of which some precede and some follow it (i.e. current growth comprised of parts of each of 2 modules of a sympodium) | peduncle subterranean, lower spathe white with vertical maroon stripes and a grey-maroon ring at top, cup-shaped, abruptly constricted at apex, c. 1.2 cm diam., keeled abaxially, faintly longitudinally ribbed | spathe limb lanceolate, c. 5 cm long × 1.5 cm wide near base, erect to slightly deflexed, light green outside, brownish maroon inside | spadix shorter than spathe, 4.5 cm long, sessile | female zone c. 3 mm long | sterile interstice c. 1.7 cm long, naked except for filiform neuter organs in lower 3 mm, very slender | neuter organs also distributed within and immediately below the female | male zone 6 mm long, 3 mm wide from side, laterally compressed | appendix sessile, c. 5 mm wide at base in lateral view, compressed, c. 2 mm wide in dorsiventral view, longitudinally ridged, rugose, tapering to a rather blunt point, chocolate brown
flower_description: pistils acroscopic | anthers cream, with connective c. twice height of thecae
fruit_description: Infructescence unknown
habitat_description: Growing in an open grassyclearing between Acacia auriculiformis/Melaleuca forest and Lophostemon lactifluusforestnear flood plain edge, in sandy well-drained soil with high water table duringwet season.
distribution_description: Known only from the Type locality.

leaf_description: Leaves several together | petiole to c. 13 cm long above ground, sheathing in subterranean part | blade deeply trilobed with linear segments to hastate to auriculate and then broadly ovate, rarely elliptic, in deeply lobed forms anterior lobe c. 14 × 1 cm and posterior lobes to 5.5 × 0.7 cm, in broad-leaved forms blade c. 7 × 3.5 cm and posterior lobes absent
inflorescence_description: Inflorescence in middle of leaf rosette | spathe base at or slightly below ground level, ovoid, c. 1 cm long, separated from limb by a rather weak constriction | limb narrowly lanceolate, c. 6--10 cm long, deep purple inside, greenish brown outside | spadix somewhat shorter than spathe, 5--9 cm long, sessile | female zone c. 2 mm long, with acroscopic pistils | sterile interstice 0.8--1 cm long, with lower 1/3--1/2 occupied by stout truncate neuter organs, the rest naked but for a tessellate pattern of flat rudiments | male zone c. 0.7 cm long, cylindric | appendix stipitate, narrowly conic, truncate at base, purple
fruit_description: Infructescence a hemispheric cluster of naked berries
habitat_description: Grows in open eucalyptwoodland and plantations at low elevation.
distribution_description: N.T., endemic to the Tiwi Is.

habit_description: Cormous herb
underground_organ_description: corm subglobose, to c. 5 cm diam
leaf_description: Leaves few together | petiole to c. 30 cm, sheathing in lower ½-2/3 | blade very narrowly lanceolate, c. 30 cm long, with margin often undulate, posterior lobes completely lacking
inflorescence_description: Inflorescence solitary, on short peduncle, directly subtended by cataphylls | spathe 10--24 cm long, abruptly constricted 3--4 cm from base | limb broadly ovate, to 20 × 10 cm, convolute in lower part | spadix shorter than spathe, to c. 10 cm long | female zone 0.5--0.8 cm long, then a 0.5 cm zone of crowded filiform neuter organs, then a 1.2--4 cm naked interstice | male zone c. 1.5 cm long | appendix sessile, narrowly conic, truncate to obtuse at base, blackish
fruit_description: Infructescence within persistent spathe base
vegetative_reproduction_description: Flowers and leaves appear to be produced simultaneously in this species, with the inflorescence appearing beside the leaves, indicating that a season’s growth consists of the fertile end of one sympodial module and the vegetative beginning of the next
habitat_description: Grows insavannah woodland and open scrub.
distribution_description: Known from the Kimberley region, W.A. and Victoria R. area, N.T.
notes: Flowers and leaves appear to be produced simultaneously in this species, with the inflorescence appearing beside the leaves, indicating that a season’s growth consists of the fertile end of one sympodial module and the vegetative beginning of the next. This is much the same as in T. taylori, T. mirabile and T. praetermissum, though in those, the timing is slightly different, so that the plants are leafless at flowering.

habit_description: Minute herb
leaf_description: Leaves 1--3 together | blade broadly ovate to elliptic, without posterior lobes, to c. 2.5 cm long
inflorescence_description: Inflorescence appearing before leaves | spathe c. 4 cm long, tubular in lower c. 1.5 cm, partly buried | tube spindle-shaped, somewhat curved, faintly constricted c. 1 cm from base | limb narrowly lanceolate, erect, greyish | spadix somewhat exceeding spathe | female zone a whorl of acroscopic pistils | neuter organs filiform, clustered at base of interstice and occupying most of lower spathe chamber, remainder of interstice naked, its apex passing through spathe tube septum | male zone shortly cylindric, situated at base of upper spathe chamber | appendix filiform, deflected through mouth of spathe tube, then erect
fruit_description: Infructescence a naked hemispheric cluster of berries c. 4 mm long
distribution_description: Endemic to Melville Is. in the N.T.

leaf_description: Leaves several together | petiole c. 13 cm long above ground, sheathing in subterranean part | blade deeply trilobed with linear segments to hastate to auriculate and then broadly ovate, rarely elliptic, in deeply lobed forms anterior lobe c. 8 × 0.5 cm and posterior lobes to 3.5 × 0.2 cm, in broad leaved forms blade c. 7 × 3.5 cm and posterior lobes reduced to absent
inflorescence_description: Inflorescence in middle of leaf rosette | spathe base at or slightly below ground level, ovoid, c. 1 cm long, separated from limb by a rather weak constriction | limb narrowly lanceolate, c. 6--10 cm long, deep purple inside, greenish brown outside | spadix somewhat shorter than spathe, 5--9 cm long, sessile | female zone c. 2 mm long, with acroscopic pistils | sterile interstice 0.8--1 cm long, with lower 1/3--1/2 occupied by rather stout clavate neuter organs, the rest naked | male zone c. 0.7 cm long, cylindric | appendix sessile, cylindric, c. 3--5 cm long, blunt-tipped, purple
fruit_description: Fruits in a hemispheric to sub-globose cluster, not protected by spathe base
habitat_description: Grows inopen woodland on ridges and near creek beds, in lateritic soil over basalt.
distribution_description: Endemic to the Mitchell Plateau, N Kimberley, W.A.

habit_description: Cormous herb
leaf_description: Leaves 2--4 | petiole 15--50 cm long, sheathing in lower 1/2 | blade not lobed, ovate to narrowly ovate, (8-) 14--34 cm long, obtuse at base
inflorescence_description: Inflorescence arising among leaves of which some precede and some follow it (i.e. current growth comprised of parts of each of 2 modules of a sympodium) | peduncle partly subterranean | spathe to 15 cm long, constricted 1.5--2.5 cm from base, spathe limb ovate, recurved and spreading at base, deep reddish purple inside, greenish outside | spadix slightly shorter than spathe | female zone c. 0.7 cm long, then a 0.4 cm zone of tangled filiform (slightly clavate) neuter organs, then a naked interstice c. (0.8-) 1.7 cm long | male zone 1.1--1.8 cm long | appendix sessile, narrowly conic, somewhat recurved, to 9.5 cm long. oblique at base, deep reddish purple
fruit_description: Infructescence within persistent spathe base
distribution_description: Known only from the type locality in the Kimberley region of W.A.
notes: Typhonium peltandroides has very distinctive striate leaf venation.

underground_organ_description: Corm compressed subglobose, c. 2.5 cm diam
leaf_description: Leaves (1-) 2 or 3 together | petiole mostly subterranean | blade (elliptic to) ovate to pedatifid with 5 sessile segments, c. 4.5 cm long, glaucous, somewhat coriaceous
inflorescence_description: Inflorescence appearing ahead of and beside current season’s leaves | spathe tubular and subterranean below constriction, septate inside at level of constriction | limb c. 4 cm long, lanceolate, purple-black inside, greyish and rugose outside, with crispate margins | spadix slightly exceeding spathe, sessile | female zone c. 3 mm long with pistils basally plagioscopic, the rest acroscopic | neuter organs clavate, down-turned, c. 3 mm long, crowded near female zone | male zone separated from neuter organs by naked interstice passing through orifice of septum, male zone c. 9 mm long, with base pressed against distal side of septum | appendix sessile, narrowly conic and distally somewhat reflexed, c. 3.5 cm long, obliquely inserted, truncate at base, rugose, blackish purple
fruit_description: Infructescence at ground level, not enclosed by spathe base, a hemispheric cluster, c. 1.5 cm diam., of ovoid to tetrahedral longitudinally ridged, somewhat rugose berries
habitat_description: Occurs in gravelly shallow lateritic soil, generally in unshaded situations inopen eucalypt woodland at low elevation.
distribution_description: Known with certainty only from the locality of the type, near Darwin, N.T.; an additional population at Karama, Darwin, may also be of this species.

habit_description: Cormous herb
leaf_description: Leaves rather numerous, to c. 11 together | petiole to c. 20 cm long, sheathing in lower 1/3 | blade deeply and narrowly trilobed with (in the only known specimen) the posterior lobes basiscopic, and anterior lobe erect, anterior lobe to c. 15 cm long, posterior lobes c. 1/2 length of anterior
inflorescence_description: Inflorescence solitary | peduncle subterranean | spathe 6.5 cm long, narrowly lanceolate, very weakly constricted at c. 1 cm from base | spadix c. 5 cm long | female zone c. 5 mm long, then a c. 2 mm zone of erect short crowded filiform neuter organs, then a naked interstice c. 1 cm long | male zone c. 0.9 cm long | appendix sessile, tapering to a point, 2.5 cm long, slender
fruit_description: Infructescence unknown
habitat_description: Growing in sandy colluviumat the base of an escarpment outlier in eucalypt forest.
distribution_description: Known only from the type.

inflorescence_description: spathe limb sharply reflexed and horizontal | interstice with neuter organs inserted along length | appendix sharply deflexed to exit mouth of spathe tube sub-horizontally and then somewhat ascending
habitat_description: Occurs in seasonally saturated sandy soil in nutrient poor grass/sedgeland with occasional Melaleuca viridiflora.
distribution_description: Known with certainty only from the locality of the type, N.T.; vegetatively similar sterile plants are reported from the E side of Howard River and from Whitewood Jungle on a tributary on the W side of Howard River.

habit_description: Rhizomatous herb
underground_organ_description: rhizome tuberous, creeping, c. 2 cm diam
leaf_description: Leaves 3 together | petiole c. 20 cm long, sheathing in lower 1/2 | blade hastosagittate, with posterior lobes equalling anterior, anterior lobe narrowly ovate, c. 7--8.5 × 6 cm, posterior lobes c. 6--8.5 × 0.9--3.4 cm
inflorescence_description: Inflorescence | peduncle c. 11 cm long | spathe 9.5 cm long, purple, lower spathe ovoid, c. 2 cm long | limb narrowly ovate, 7 × 3.5 cm | spadix 6.5 cm long | female zone c. 5 mm long | sterile interstice 1.6 cm long with crowded filiform neuter organs in lower 0.6 cm and scattered shorter ones in the rest | male zone slender, 1.5 × 0.2 cm | appendix sessile, cylindric, 2.5 × 0.2 cm long
fruit_description: Infructescence unknown
habitat_description: Occurs on the edge of open Eucalyptus tetradonta woodland.
distribution_description: Known only from the type locality, N Qld.
notes: Evidently closely related to T. eliosurum (q.v.), from which it is widely disjunct in habitat and geographically, this species differs in the relatively longer male zone, shorter appendix and less acuminate spathe.

habit_description: Cormous herb
underground_organ_description: corm subglobose to flattish, somewhat irregular, c. 4 cm diam
leaf_description: Leaves to 6 together | petiole 15--50 cm long | blade hastate with posterior lobes somewhat raised, somewhat glaucous, occasionally variegated in an irregularly spattered pattern of paler greyish green, anterior lobe broadly ovate to lanceolate, c. 10--20 × 2--8 cm, posterior lobes about 1/2 length of anterior
inflorescence_description: Inflorescence | peduncle much shorter than petioles | spathe c. 12.5--33 cm long, lower spathe ovoid, c. 4 cm long, green, separated from limb by abrupt constriction | limb broadly ovate, slightly reflexed, somewhat convolute in lower part, deep purple inside, outside greenish suffused brown with midrib whitish | spadix somewhat to much shorter than spathe, c. 9 cm long | female zone 1 cm long | sterile interstice c. 2.5 cm long, c. 0.3 cm diam., with blackish purple filiform neuter organs in lower part, the rest occupied by shorter subpyramidal neuter organs | male zone equalling sterile zone | appendix shortly stipitate, narrowly conic, obliquely truncate at base, c. 3.5 × 0.8 cm, blunt-tipped, deep purple-black
flower_description: stamens whitish, maroon near pores
fruit_description: Infructescence within persistent spathe base
habitat_description: Grows in eucalypt and she-oak woodland.
distribution_description: From N Qld in scattered localities from Restoration Is., Cape York Penin., S to Palm Cove, Atherton Tableland, and Turtle Is. (mouth of Styx R.).
notes: This species is distinguished from T. weipanum and T. eliosurum by the flattish, irregularly subglobose corm and truncate-based, blunt-tipped appendix.

flowering_time_description: Flowers Sept. and possibly in other months
leaf_description: Fronds boat-shaped, 0.5--0.8 mm long, 0.2--0.4 mm wide, 1.7--2.5 times as long as wide, whitish green with more intensely green margins, with 8--10 (-25) stomata
phenology_text: Flowers Sept. and possibly in other months.
habitat_description: Eutrophic, grows in quiet waters in warm temperate to tropical regions.
distribution_description: Occurs in W.A., N.T., S.A., Qld, N.S.W. and Vic.; also in Malaysia, Singapore and possibly India.

leaf_description: Fronds boat-shaped, 0.5--1.3 mm long, 0.3--0.8 mm wide, 1.3--2 times as long as wide, bright green, with 50--80 stomata
habitat_description: Mesotrophic to eutrophic; found in quiet waters in suboceanic, temperate regions.
distribution_description: Occurs in S.A., N.S.W., Vic. and Tas.; also in New Zealand.
notes: For information about the flowers of this species see: F.A. Bernard et al., Bull. Torrey Bot. Club 117: 18--26 (1990) and E. Landolt, Ber. Geobot. Inst. E.T.H. Stiftung Rübel Zürich 58: 132--137 (1992).

habit_description: Robust herb, at first stalkless, later with erect, thick stalk to 1 m or more high
leaf_description: Leaves with petiole to 1 m long | lamina broadly sagittate, 40--80 cm long, 30--70 cm wide, with 1--4 clear marginal veins | upper lobe twice as long as lateral lobes
inflorescence_description: Inflorescence peduncles to c. 20 cm long | spathe 13--15 cm long, usually greenish white, lower portion ovoid and 6--7 cm long, constricted above pistillate flowers | Spadix staminate to apex, c. ⅔-¾ as long as spathe
distribution_description: On Christmas Island introduced by the Chinese for cultivation for its edible, starchy tubers. It has become naturalised in several places on the island, especially in damper areas, and sometimes marks the sites of disused gardens. Probably originated in the New World tropics, now commonly cultivated and naturalised throughout the tropics. (Du Puy 1993: 439). On Norfolk Island this species has established itself on the Island as an escape from cultivation near the Melanesian Mission. The exact origin of Xanthosoma sagittifolium is uncertain but it is now commonly cultivated throughout the tropics. (Green 1994: 418).
notes: The white sap is a skin irritant. The tubers, although edible, are considered inferior to those of the somewhat similar Colocasia esculenta (Taro), which differs in its distinctly peltate leaves. (Du Puy 1993: 439). Also used in traditional medicine.

common_name: Arum Lily, Calla Lily, White Arum, White Arum Lily, Lily of the Nile, Death Lily, and others.
habit_description: Robust evergreen rhizomatous herb, clump-forming
leaf_description: Leaves several together, glabrous | petiole to 1.2 (-1.5) m long, fleshy, sheathing in lower ⅓-½ | sheath persistent | blade hastosagittate, to 50 (-60) cm long and 20 (-30) cm wide, slightly leathery, dull mid green to somewhat glossy dark green (to somewhat glaucous) | the tip bent downwards or curling towards back of leaf
inflorescence_description: Peduncle equal to or slightly longer than petioles | Inflorescence solitary, rarely 2 together, produced in sequence interspersed with foliage leaves | spathe to c. 25 cm long, trumpet-shaped, with limb spreading and distally reflexed, white to cream, green at base, sometimes green in the upper third | spadix sessile, about half as long as the spathe | male zone golden (stamens and staminodes yellow-orange), lower spathe persistent in fruit, becoming green | limb marcescent
flower_description: pistils interspersed with staminodes
fruit_description: Berries irregularly globose, 5--10 mm long, green, ripening yellow-orange | Infructescence protected by persistent spathe base
phenology_text: Flowers late winter, spring and sporadically into summer.
ecology_description: Persists around habitations; garden escape; environmental weed. An invasive weed with impacts on the environment, biodiversity and agriculture.
habitat_description: Grows in open or semi-shaded marshy places and creek banks with high nutrient levels. Invades pastures, moist gullies, roadsides, wasteland, rubbish tips, wetlands, waterways (disturbed creeklines, stream banks, floodways, drains, irrigation ditches) and bushland.
distribution_description: Native to S Africa (Cape, Natal and Transvaal provinces) and Lesotho; widely naturalised in cooler areas in Australia in W.A., S.A., N.S.W., Norfolk Is., Vic. and Tas.
notes: Arum Lily is poisonous, as well as being a skin and eye irritant, to humans, livestock and pets. Especially toxic to children. See Shepherd (2004), McKenzie (2012). See Green (1994: 416) for flora treatment for the species occurring on Norfolk Island where naturalised beside one or two streams as an escape from cultivation.

habit_description: Tree to 6 m high, with a single trunk or with few branches towards top, with brittle wood
leaf_description: Leaf lamina oblanceolate, (15-) 20--25 (-35) cm long, (4.5-) 6--7 (-9.5) cm broad, narrowed at base, acute to obtuse
inflorescence_description: Inflorescence with numerous flower clusters, male clusters 15--25 cm long, 4--7-flowered, female clusters stouter, 10--15 cm long, 3- or 4-flowered
flower_description: Calyx abortive, or a rim in female flowers | Petals broadly triangular, 4 in male flowers, 6 or 7 in female, 1--1.5 mm long, persistent | Stamens 4 | anthers c. 0.7 mm long | Ovary flask-shaped, 4--5 mm long, 5--7-locular | styles 5--7, 2 mm long, becoming strongly recurved
fruit_description: Fruit globose, 7--8 mm long, bluntly 5--7-ribbed
ecology_description: See Director of National Parks (2010: 100) and references therein for details on population number, recorded sites, threats and management strategies.
habitat_description: There are relatively few plants, not all in the National Park, scattered in wooded areas and in need of conservation.
distribution_description: Norfolk Island. Endemic and rare.

habit_description: Tree 5--6 m high, with single trunk or with few branches towards top, with brittle wood
leaf_description: Leaves | lamina broadly oblanceolate, distinctly large, 50--75 cm long, 25--30 cm wide, gradually narrowed and finally rounded at base, obtuse to rounded at apex
inflorescence_description: Male inflorescence not seen | Female inflorescence terminal, paniculate, 10--15 cm long, densely clustered
flower_description: Calyx rudimentary | Petals 5 or 6, narrowly triangular, 1.5--2 mm long, persistent | Stamens as many as petals, c. 1 mm long | Ovary flask-shaped, 3--4 mm long, 5- or 6-locular | styles 5 or 6, 2--3 mm long, strongly recurved, persistent
fruit_description: Fruit globose, 5--6 mm long, bluntly 5- or 6-ribbed
ecology_description: The effective reproductive population is determined by the limited number of mature female plants; see Director of National Parks (2010: 101) and references therein for details on population numbers, plantings, threats and management strategies.
habitat_description: Can grow on steep slopes, coastal cliffs, and in both shaded and unshaded sites, and is most commonly established at the edges of canopy gaps or along forest margins, but sometimes also beneath pines (Sykes & Atkinson 1988).
distribution_description: Endemic to Norfolk Island.

leaflet_count_description: leaflets (7-) 11 or 13, narrowly ovate to lanceolate, strongly oblique, (3-) 4--8 (-10) cm long, (1.5-) 1.8--2.5 (-4.5) cm wide, acute at base, coarsely crenulate-dentate, especially upper margin, acute to acuminate at apex, light green
habit_description: Tree to 12 m or more high, dioecious
leaf_description: Leaves imparipinnate, 10--35 cm long | leaflets (7-) 11 or 13, narrowly ovate to lanceolate, strongly oblique, (3-) 4--8 (-10) cm long, (1.5-) 1.8--2.5 (-4.5) cm wide, acute at base, coarsely crenulate-dentate, especially upper margin, acute to acuminate at apex, light green
inflorescence_description: Inflorescence terminal, paniculate, 10--30 cm long, umbellules 4--7 (-9)-flowered | pedicels 2--3 mm long, articulated at base of flowers
flower_description: Petals (4 or) 5, triangular, yellow, becoming reflexed | Stamens c. 2 mm long | Ovary 2-locular | styles 2, basally united, c. 1 mm long
fruit_description: Fruit laterally compressed-spheroidal, 3.5--4.5 (-5) mm long, bluntly ribbed, purple-maroon to brown
dispersal_description: Seeds dispersed by birds
ecology_description: Seeds dispersed by birds.
habitat_description: On Lord Howe Island a fairly common tree mainly in sheltered forest in the lowland areas; to 400 m alt. Usually in sheltered forest, on basalt and calcarenite soil (Department of Environment and Climate Change (NSW) 2007 - Appendices page 204).
distribution_description: Occurs on Lord Howe Island; also native to New Caledonia and Vanuatu.

common_name: Black Kauri, Purple Kauri, Blue Kauri.
habit_description: Tree to 50 m high
bark_description: Bark smooth, purplish black or reddish purple to brown or grey brown, shedding in coarse scales
leaf_description: leaves and cones sometimes glaucous when young | Leaves with petiole 1--2 mm long | lamina linear to elliptic, 3--7 cm long, 5--20 mm wide
habitat_description: Confined to submontane rainforests.
distribution_description: A rare species occurring in north-eastern Qld.
notes: See Australian Tropical Rainforest Plants and The Gymnosperm Database.

habit_description: Tree to 50 m high
bark_description: Bark brown to grey-brown, shedding in coarse scales
leaf_description: Leaves with petiole 1--2 mm long | lamina linear to elliptic, 2--9 cm long, 5--25 mm wide
habitat_description: Confined to rainforest.
distribution_description: A rare species, occurring on the Atherton Tableland and in nearby ranges in north-eastern Qld.
notes: See The Gymnosperm Database.

habit_description: Tree to 50 m high
bark_description: Bark smooth, orange-brown, brown or grey, shedding in broad scales
leaf_description: Leaves with petiole 3--10 mm long | lamina linear to elliptic, 5--13 cm long, 1--4 cm wide
habitat_description: Found in rainforest.
distribution_description: This species has two disjunct areas of distribution: in the Cook and Kennedy districts of northern Qld, and at Wide Bay, south-eastern Qld. Disjunct occurrences have been recognised as subsp. nesophila Whitmore in New Guinea and New Britain.
notes: See The Gymnosperm Database and Australian Tropical Rainforest Plants.

common_name: Bunya Pine, Bunya Bunya, Queensland Pine.
habit_description: Tree to 50 m high, crown dome-shaped
leaf_description: Adult leaves dimorphic, narrowly triangular to acicular on orthotropic shoots, narrowly triangular on plagiotropic shoots, broadly based, decurrent, spreading and secondarily distichous, 1--5 cm long, 3--10 mm wide, glossy, dark green above, paler below | apex sharply pointed
inflorescence_description: bract-scales winged
seed_description: Seeds ovoid, 20--25 mm long, 15--20 mm diam., shed from scales at maturity
habitat_description: Locally abundant in tall, montane rainforests in deep soils. Often an emergent tree above the rainforest canopy.
distribution_description: Endemic to Qld; known from two disjunct occurrences, one near Mount Molloy in the north-east and one near Gympie and inland from there in the south-east.
notes: The large falling cones have proven a hazard in public park and avenue plantings, and many trees have since been removed. See also Araucaria bidwillii in The Gymnosperm Database: https://www.conifers.org/ (accessed 5 March 2024).

common_name: Hoop Pine, Morton Bay Pine, Dorrigo Pine, Colonial Pine.
habit_description: Tree to 50 m high
leaf_description: Adult leaves incurved, subulate, keeled, 6--8 mm long
inflorescence_description: bract scales winged
seed_description: Seeds retained on scale when shed
habitat_description: Grows in drier rainforests and on beach dunes.
distribution_description: Locally a frequent emergent in drier rainforests on hilly or rocky sites from northern Cape York Peninsula, Qld, to the Bellinger River, north-eastern N.S.W., and on beach dunes in northern Qld.
notes: See also Araucaria cunninghamii in The Gymnosperm Database: https://www.conifers.org/ (accessed 5 March 2024).

habit_description: Tree to 70 m high with trunk to 2 m diam
stem_description: Branches horizontal | ultimate shoots horizontal or somewhat pendulous | shoots, including leaves, 7--10 mm diam
leaf_description: Mature leaves in imbricate series encircling stems, broadly ovate, 4--7 mm long, 3--6 mm wide, minutely ciliolate, with slightly incurved, blunt, horny apex
seed_description: Seeds 2.5--3 cm long, 1.3--1.5 cm wide
phenology_text: Heavy coning is intermittent, occurring every three to five years.
ecology_description: Besides Lord Howe Island, self-propagating plants are also occurring in coastal areas of mainland Australia, on foreshores, headlands, in parks and avenues. Wind and salt tolerant, and able to grow in deep coastal sands (Rodd 1996).
habitat_description: Forests and open areas at all elevations from coastal to peaks.
distribution_description: Endemic to Norfolk Island and is frequent in the National Park and elsewhere; becoming naturalised on Lord Howe Island where it has become self-sown beside the lagoon, between the beach and the road.
notes: See also Araucaria heterophylla in The Gymnosperm Database: https://www.conifers.org/

ecology_description: On Christmas Island, Robber crabs (Birgus latro) gather around fallen palm trees to eat the starchy core of the trunk. In order to collect the crabs for a meal or for fishing bait, an Arenga palm is sometimes felled and the trunk split open, attracting large numbers of crabs a few days later. The crabs also relish the ripe fruit, gathering around the base of a fruiting palm to eat the fruit as it falls, some even climb up to the inflorescences. The fruit is also a favourite of the endemic Christmas Island Imperial Pigeon (Ducula whartoni). It is perhaps surprising that these animals are not affected by the highly irritant sap of the fruit, which contains large quantities of minute sharp crystals which cause intense itching and discomfort if accidentally rubbed into the skin.
habitat_description: Sometimes gregarious, forming almost pure stands on basaltic outcrops where there is usually more moisture in the soil, especially in the shorter forest onthe terraces. Also frequent as an undercanopy tree throughout the taller rainforest on the plateau and terraces, with the juveniles forming important elements of the shrub layer.
distribution_description: Endemic to Christmas Island.
notes: A distinctive species, possibly related to Arenga porphyrocarpa (H.Mart.) H.E.Moore or A. microcarpa Becc. Shares the monocarpic habit with A. pinnata, the Sugar Palm (which otherwise differs in many characters), an economically important palm for its sugary sap and the large reserve of starch built up in the trunk prior to flowering and fruiting. Arenga listeri could have similar commercial properties. The female inflorescences sometimes rupture the base of the leaf sheath, but most develop after the leaves have fallen to expose the stem and buds. Typically, the most apical inflorescence is female and develops first. Then the central buds at the nodes develop, again as females, and finally the lateral buds of the nodes develop sequentially into male inflorescences as the tree gradually dies.
