notes: Distinguished from perennial species by its smaller flowers, from the perennials and Bulbine alata in having hairs on only 3 stamens, reddish or brownish anthers and smaller capsules, and from B. alata by its wingless seeds. Variable in habit, leaf size and shape, flower size, anther and style orientation and anther colour. Some populations from Tas. and southern coastal mainland appear to be facultatively perennial. The species forms part of a large, taxonomically difficult polyploid complex. Although Bulbine semibarbata and B. alata , the two tetraploid but functionally diploid taxa so far identified at the base of the complex, are differentiated chromosomally and morphologically, intermediates occur over a wide area. These appear to result from some hybridisation and introgression at the 'diploid' level and extensive hybridisation among auto- and allo-polyploid derivatives. Patterns of variation may also have been affected by some cryptic speciation at higher ploidy levels, especially in W.A. In Fl. Centr. Australia 423 (1981), J.P.Jessop distinguished Bulbine semibarbata var. A chiefly on the basis that the pedicels recurved after flowering. Cytological studies show that this character occurs irregularly in disjunct and chromosomally differing populations. Taxonomic segregation on this basis therefore seems inappropriate. It is possible, however, that the Pilbara populations in W.A., where the pedicel is recurved in flower as well as in fruit, may be found to merit separate status.

Some likely hybrids including the types of A. attenuatum var. multilobum F.Muell and A. paleaceum var. prenticei Baker, originate from localities from beyond the southernmost limit of A. paleaceum near Maryborough, Queensland. Asplenium attenuatum var. attenuatum also hybridises with A. polyodon G.Forst. to produce plants with sparsely scaly rachises and long attenuate pinnae that have been described as A. attenuatum var. schneideri F.M.Bailey (Ohlsen et al. 2014).

notes: Originally collected by J.J. Lister in 1887, probably near Flying Fish Cove, Christmas Island. It was not collected by C.W. Andrews, but Ridley (1906), reported having found a single small specimen at Toms Ladder, again in Flying Fish Cove (DuPuy 1993). These historical collections have been lost, and there had been some mystery concerning the identity of this species (DuPuy 1993). Baker (1890) described the plant as having pinnate fronds c. 10--13 cm long, c. 2.5--4 cm wide, with stipes c. 5--7.5 cm long. He described the pinnae as being deeply lobed, with the sori confined to the lobes, leaving the central regions of the pinnae sterile and naked. Du Puy (1993) neotypified the species based on a collection made by him that was the only known specimen at the time that closely matched the description of A. listeri given by Baker (1890). During years with greater rainfall and a less pronounced dry season plants can attain much larger dimensions than plants in typical or dry years. Such plants are included as upper extremes in the description. Most collections made of this species on Christmas Island were taken in the dry season, including those of Lister and are much smaller.

notes: Asplenium milnei is one of several closely related species that form a polyploid complex that has been called the Austral group (Perrie & Brownsey 2005; Ohlsen et al. 2014). The Austral group has its centre of diversity in New Zealand where numerous hybrid combinations between the species of the Austral group have been reported, but no hybrids are known there between the Austral group and other Asplenium lineages (Brownsey 1977; Brownsey & Perrie 2018). A hybrid (J. Pickard 2711, K, NSW) was reported between A. milnei and A. polyodon G.Forst., on Lord Howe Island (Green 1988), which is the first putative instance of hybridisation of an Austral group species with another Asplenium lineage. In addition, a hybrid with A. surrogatum P.S.Green has once been collected (Green 1994). This was by Chris Goudey from beside the track to Boat Harbour (Green 1994).

Hybrids between A. paleaceum and A. attenuatum have been collected several times (Ohlsen et al. 2014, also see A. attenuatum var. attenuatum profile). A few collections, however, appear identical to A. paleaceum but have aborted spores e.g. Carlisle Island, P.R. Sharpe 4503 et al. (BRI); Mount Dryander, 27 May 1969, L.S. Smith (BRI); Chester River, J.R. Clarkson 2347 (BRI). It is uncertain whether these are apomictic forms, hybrids of an unknown origin or if like in some other fern genera such as Pyrrosia (Hovenkamp 1986) plants that are not hybrids still produce aborted or abnormal spores along with only few fertile spores. notes: Asplenium surrogatum along with the other Lord Howe Island endemic species, A. milnei Carruth. in B.C.Seemann and A. pteridioides Baker, are the three descendants of a common ancestor (i.e. they form a clade) making it possible that these three species originated in close proximity on Lord Howe Island (Papadopulos et al. 2011; Ohlsen et al. 2014). This Lord Howe Island group is derived from within a clade comprised of numerous Asplenium species including the nest-forming, bird-nest Asplenium (e.g. A. australasicum (J.Sm.) Hook.) and a polyploid species complex in New Zealand and southern Australia that includes A. gracillimum Colenso (Ohlsen et al. 2014; Xu et al. 2020). Apart from Asplenium surrogatum and a dubious count for an Asian species, all chromosome counts reported for species of this large clade are tetraploid or higher (Schneider et al. 2017). This implies that if the diploid count reported for A. surrogatum in Tindale & Roy (2002) is correct it has arisen by a halving a chromosome numbers, which is not yet known in Asplenium, or there has been numerous independent cases of polyploidy from diploid ancestors within this clade (Schneider et al. 2017), which seems unlikely given the lack of putative diploid counts. Consequently, the count reported in Tindale and Roy (2002), which was not supported by an accompanying microphotograph of a squash displaying the chromosomes, is suspect and requires confirmation.

notes: H.N. Ridley, Journal of the Straits Branch of the Royal Asiatic Society 45: 146, 148, 153, 219--220 (1906) described this as a new species, endemic on Christmas Island, but it cannot be distinguished from B. abbreviata. He also noted that the minute fruits are wind dispersed.

distribution_description: Native to E tropical Africa. Naturalised on granite outcrops in SW Western Australia and SE New South Wales, also recorded from South Australia, Victoria and Tasmania as an occasional garden escape, probably from dumped garden waste.

common_name: Busy Lizzie, Zanzibar Balsam, Patient Lucy.
habit_description: Herb, perennial, to 1 m high (usually less than 0.5 m high)
stem_description: stems succulent, rooting at the lower nodes, glabrous or rarely slightly pubescent at shoot apices
leaf_description: Leaves alternate | lamina ovate to broadly ovate, 3--11 cm long, 10--50 mm wide, sometimes reddish below, glabrous, with 5--8 pairs of lateral veins | margin coarsely toothed | apex acuminate | petiole 10--40 mm long, not or scarcely winged, with scattered, thick-stalked glands
inflorescence_description: Inflorescences axillary, usually 2 or 3 (-5)-flowered | peduncles 2--5 cm long | Pedicels 10--30 mm long, slender, bracteate | bracts linear-lanceolate or subulate, acute, c. 2 mm long
flower_description: Flowers mostly pink to red or orange, sometimes white, with face flat, spur white, 3--4.5 cm long | Sepals, lowermost sepal 8--15 mm long, whitish, with spur 20--35 mm long | lateral sepals 3--7 mm long, green | Petals 10--20 mm long, uppermost petal largest, keeled | lateral petals fused towards base
fruit_description: Capsule glabrous, fusiform, weakly 5-ribbed, swollen in the middle, 15--20 mm long, c. 3 mm wide
seed_description: Seeds tuberculate
habitat_description: Disturbed areas in moist, shaded woodland, eucalypt forest and margins of rainforest, often near creeks, on roadsides and near settlements; garden escape and spread from the dumping of garden refuse.
distribution_description: Native to tropical east and southern Africa, from Kenya to Mozambique. Naturalised in numerous locations in Queensland, New South Wales, and possibly on Norfolk Island.
notes: Very variable in habit and flower colour.

flower_colour_description: mostly pink; mostly red; mostly orange

common_name: Madeira Vine, Lamb's Tail, Mignonette Vine, Jalap; many names in many languages, see entries in Bibliography.
profile_author: L.W. Jessup, R.L. Barrett, R.O. Makinson, P.G. Kodela
habit_description: Twining vine, with root-crown tuber, and often developing aerial tubers from leaf axils
stem_description: Aerial stems usually less than 10 m long but recorded to 40 m
leaf_description: Leaves alternate | lamina ovate or broadly ovate to cordate, 2--15 cm long, 1--12 cm wide, cordate at base, entire, acute to obtuse or sometimes shortly acuminate or emarginate at apex, fleshy to succulent, glossy above, glabrous | petiole 0.5--2 cm long
inflorescence_description: Racemes pendulous, 6--25 (-30) cm long | Pedicels 3--4 mm long | bracts subulate to narrowly ovate, 1.5--2.5 mm long
flower_description: flowers numerous, sweet-scented | Tepals ovate or ovate-oblong to elliptic, obtuse, c. 2--3 mm long, spreading, white to cream | Stamens 2--2.5 mm long, ascending, strongly divergent | filaments c. 1 mm wide at base, tapering to anther | Style shallowly or deeply trifid | stigmas clavate
fruit_description: Fruit an indehiscent, subglobular capsule
seed_description: Seed 1, globular, smooth (fruit and seed-set uncommon in Australia)
ecology_description: For details on biology and ecology see Vivian-Smith et al. (2007, 2009) and references therein.
habitat_description: Disturbed areas, usually establishing in new areas from stem fragments and aerial tubers often in garden waste. The aerial tubers readily break off and fragment, sprouting rapidly in moist shady microsites. Young vines rapidly climb over shrubs, rock outcrops, and small (and sometimes large) trees. Often favours high light-level patches in moist vegetation types, e.g. margins and canopy breaks in rainforest, streamside gallery forest, creek embankments. Very persistent once established.
distribution_description: Native to tropical South America, now cultivated and naturalised in many tropical and subtropical countries. In Australian still sometimes cultivated, aggressively weedy and naturalised in Western Australia, South Australia, Queensland, New South Wales, Victoria, Tasmania; also on Lord Howe and Norfolk Islands.
notes: The species is an aggressive environmental weed, with a still-expanding range in several jurisdictions. Anredera cordifolia may rapidly smother native vegetation, can collapse tree canopies, and in dense infestations may act as a transformer weed, modifying the microenvironment by either reduction of light and air movement, or (after canopy collapse) by creation of light gaps favouring further weed invasion. Anredera cordifolia is a declared weed in various jurisdictions or regions thereof. As at December 2020, A. cordifolia is:Included on the Commonwealth Weeds of National Significance (WONS) list.A ‘State Priority Weed’ in New South Wales.A ‘restricted invasive plant’ in Queensland.A ‘restricted weed’ in Victoria.A ‘declared weed’ in Tasmania.A ‘declared plant’ in South Australia.A ‘Class C Declared Weed’ in the Northern Territory. Anredera cordifolia is listed as an exemplar species of ‘Invasion and establishment of exotic vines and scramblers as a Key Threatening Process' (NSW TSSC 2006). For an account of Anredera cordifolia occurring on Norfolk and Lord Howe Islands see Green (1994: 90--91).

common_name: Ceylon Spinach, Remajong, Indian Spinach, Malabar Spinach, Creeping Spinach.
habit_description: Twining herbaceous vine or sometimes procumbent (creeping herb)
stem_description: stems 2--10 m long, succulent, pale green to purplish red, glabrous, mucilaginous, short-lived
leaf_description: Leaves | lamina usually ovate (often broadly so) to circular, 5--15 cm long, 2.5--12 cm wide, cuneate to cordate at base, entire, obtuse to shortly acuminate at apex, glabrous | petiole 1--3 cm long
inflorescence_description: Inflorescence axillary, spicate, un- or few-branched | spikes long-pedunculate, 5--28 cm long, succulent | bracts small, acute, persistent
flower_description: Flowers fleshy, white to purple-pink, urceolate, not or scarcely opening (cleistogamous or nearly so) | sepals 2, petalloid, obtuse, adnate to the perianth, persistent | Perianth 3--5 mm long, broad-tubular with an inflated base, 5-lobed towards the apex | lobes rounded | Stamens inserted near top of perianth, not emergent | Style tripartite to near base | stigmas 3, linear
fruit_description: Fruit tightly enclosed by the persistent fleshy perianth, globose, 4--8 mm diam., appearing shallowly 4-lobed, black, glossy
seed_description: Seeds 1, globular
ecology_description: This species is salt-tolerant, and has been collected from habitats that are open to sea-spray.
habitat_description: Sporadically naturalised, usually in disturbed areas, including shrubland; often associated with market gardens.
distribution_description: Native to the Old World tropics, probably originating in east Africa, but now so widely cultivated throughout the tropics that its precise origin has been obscured. Naturalised in Queensland, New South Wales, Tasmania and on Christmas Island.
notes: For account of Basella alba occurring on Christmas Island see Du Puy (1993: 122--123).

habit_description: Monoecious shrub 20--70 cm high
leaf_description: Leaves obovoid, obtusely trigonous in cross-section, 4--15 mm long, 1--1.5 mm wide, rounded acute
flower_description: Male flowers axillary or terminal, sessile, subtended when young by 2 concave bracts up to 4 mm long and 2 mm wide with membranous margins, the 2 united bracteoles forming a campanulate structure | staminal filaments linear, terete, 2--2.5 mm long | anthers elliptic, c. 1 mm long, the connective distinctly protruding | staminodes 1.5--2.5 mm long, 0.5--1 mm wide | Female flowers solitary (sometimes one fertile male flower between two female flowers at apex of branchlet or with only one axillary female flower and an apical fertile male flower), sessile, obliquely ovoid-ellipsoidal, 4--7 mm long, 1.5--3 mm wide, abaxial locules smaller than adaxial | stigmas sessile, papillate
fruit_description: Fruit an oblique fleshy drupe up to 11 mm long and 5 mm wide
seed_description: Seeds 5--5.5 mm long, 1.1--1.2 mm wide
habitat_description: Grows onsaline mud flats, often in association with Halosarciaspp. behind the mangrove community.
distribution_description: Occurs along the Australian coast from near Broome, W.A. to Princess Charlotte Bay on Cape York Peninsula, Qld.
notes: Batis argillicola may be recognised by its fleshy leaves, unisexual flowers, and distinctive fruits and seeds. The Australian material referred to B. argillicola differs from the New Guinea material in having differently shaped leaves, different inflorescence characters, sessile male flowers, and terete (not winged) staminal filaments.

fruiting_time_description: Flowers (late winter-) spring; fruits mature in summer
leaflet_count_description: leaflets (3-) 5--11 (-19), ovate (-lanceolate) or obliquely ovate, to 10 (-14) cm long, to 5 (-6) cm wide, glossy or duller bluish green above, paler and dull beneath
habit_description: Shrub to 3 m high or more, often suckering underground
leaf_description: Leaves to 30 (-40) cm long | leaflets (3-) 5--11 (-19), ovate (-lanceolate) or obliquely ovate, to 10 (-14) cm long, to 5 (-6) cm wide, glossy or duller bluish green above, paler and dull beneath | margin flat or undulate | coarsely toothed with 8--35 spines
inflorescence_description: Racemes 4--8 (-19) cm long, in fascicles of 3--5 or more | Pedicel to 10 mm long
flower_description: stigma sessile
fruit_description: Fruit globose or subglobose, c. 6 mm long, blue to dark blue, pruinose
phenology_text: Flowers (late winter-) spring; fruits mature in summer.
ecology_description: Potential weed, garden escape.
distribution_description: Naturalised at Wirrabara, South Australia (since at least 1988), scattered in eastern New South Wales (including near Dorrigo, the Blue Mountains, Southern Highlands, near Bega and the Southern Tablelands), and in the Australian Capital Territory (since at least 1993); native to the W coast of North America from British Columbia into California. There are records of uncertain status from Victoria and Tasmania.
notes: B.D. Morley, Flora of Australia 2: 359--362 (2007) describes the possibility of hybridisation, both in the wild and in cultivation, with taxa such as Berberis repens Lindl.

flowering_time_description: Flowers (late winter-) spring; fruits mature in summer [parenthetical extremes]
Flowers (late winter-) spring; fruits mature in summer

habit_description: Shrub to 3.5 m high
stem_description: branchlets subterete, red-brown, shortly pilose, with spines
leaf_description: Leaves evergreen | lamina obovate to obovate-oblong, 1--2 cm long, 0.5--1.5 cm wide, cuneate at base, remotely spiny-toothed at margin, 3-spined at apex, thick, rigid, glossy dark green above, paler green below | spines slender | 3- or 5-partite, 3--10 mm long
inflorescence_description: pedicel 6--10 mm long, red
flower_description: Flowers golden, flushed with red | style to 4 mm long, persistent
fruit_description: Fruit globose, c. 6--7 mm long, dark blue, pruinose when ripe
ecology_description: Potential weed, garden escape.
distribution_description: Naturalised in the Mount Wilson area, New South Wales, and the Dandenongs, Victoria, since at least 1932 and 1977 respectively; also reported from South Australia and Tasmania; native to Chile and Argentina.

habit_description: Shrub to 5 m high, often multistemmed
stem_description: branchlets terete or subterete, yellowish, glabrous
leaf_description: Leaves semi-deciduous | lamina elliptic or ovate to ovate-elliptic, sometimes obovate to narrowly obovate, (2-) 2.5--6.5 cm long, (0.8-) 1.2--2.4 cm wide, attenuate, entire to spinulose at margin (coarsely serrate in summer shoots), acuminate, chartaceous, dull green above, paler yellow-green below | spines absent or 1--3-partite | to 15 (-20) mm long
inflorescence_description: pedicel to 7 mm long, yellowish
flower_description: Flowers pale yellow | style 2--5 mm long, persistent
fruit_description: Fruit oblong to ellipsoidal, c. 7--9 mm long, dark purple-red or purplish, pruinose when ripe
germination_description: Chitriae suggests that some naturalised Australian specimens have possibly arisen as seedlings from garden plants
habitat_description: Usually disturbed areas, recorded growing in weedy shrubland, woodland and open eucalypt forest; sometimes forming thickets.
distribution_description: Naturalised in the Yerranderie and Tenterfield areas of New South Wales since at least 1953; also recorded from the Katoomba area and other localised records, including a single plant from Mount Ainslie in the Australian Capital Territory (A.J. Whalen 170 & A.M. Lyne, CANB, MEL, NSW); a native of Nepal.
notes: This species has been commonly distributed and grown in cultivation erroneously as 'Berberis aristata', (L.W.A. Ahrendt, Journal of the Linnean Society, Botany 57: 1--410, 1961). Berberis aristata DC. from Nepal is very rare in cultivation and its identity is obscure. Berberis floribunda, B. glaucocarpa Stapf from India and Nepal, and B. chitria Hort. (non Lindl., nom. illeg.) are closely allied to B. aristata, and are all more common in cultivation than it. Berberis glaucocarpa is even naturalised in the United Kingdom. The naturalised taxon at Yerranderie, New South Wales, is here referred to B. floribunda (not B. aristata as in N.C.W. Beadle et al., Flora of the Sydney Region 148, 1982) and is an escape from cultivation. The material (D. Brown 16) with larger leaves from Tenterfield, New South Wales, is closer to B. chitria, which is also in cultivation. The variation patterns of critical characters of species and recorded hybrids within subsect. Chitriae suggests that some naturalised Australian specimens have possibly arisen as seedlings from garden plants. This accounts for the difficulty in identifying material, and the character expression found in a genus of species notorious for hybridity and having seeds distributed by birds.

common_name: Japanese Barberry, Thunberg's Barberry, Barberry, Red Barberry.
habit_description: Deciduous shrub to 4 m high, often dense, multistemmed
leaf_description: Leaves spathulate to elliptic or obovate (sometimes appearing rhombic- or diamond-shaped), 10--35 (-45) mm long, 5--15 (-22) mm wide, thin, glabrous | venation obscure | upper surface green or yellow-green, dull | lower surface paler or greyish | base tapering | margin entire | apex rounded or obtuse | petiole indistinct due to tapering lamina, to c. 8 mm long

fruit_description: Berries ellipsoid, to 8 mm long, to 4.5 mm wide, maturing red or orange-red, shiny, without a bloom
habitat_description: At Mount Wilson occurs in the understorey of tall open eucalypt forest, on basalt.
distribution_description: Native to Japan and E Asia. In Australia, Berberis thunbergii has been recorded locally naturalised at Mount Wilson in the Blue Mountains, New South Wales; see Hosking et al. (2003) for details. There is a record of uncertain status from Victoria, viz. near Howan's Gap Alpine Centre, 8 Dec. 1999, I.C. Clarke s.n. (MEL).

common_name: Common Barberry, Barberry, Barberry Bush, European Barberry, Jaundice Berry.

stem_description: stems glabrous, dimorphic with elongate primary and short axillary shoots

flower_description: Flowers c. 5 mm diam. | perianth yellow
fruit_description: Berry obloid to ovoid, 9--12 mm long, ripening bright red, retaining sessile stigma
seed_description: seeds 1--3
ecology_description: Potential invasive weed and alternate host for Wheat Rust Puccinia graminis.
distribution_description: Native of Europe. Sparingly naturalised in New South Wales; potential localised garden escapes in other states.

common_name: Sacred Bamboo, Heavenly Bamboo, Japanese Sacred Bamboo, Nanten.
fruiting_time_description: Flowers mainly (September-) November-December; fruits mainly April-July
habit_description: Shrub to 2 (-3) m high

flower_description: Flowers to 5--7.5 mm diam., with white petals and prominent yellow anthers
fruit_description: Berry globose, 6--10 mm diam., bright red
phenology_text: Flowers mainly (September-) November-December; fruits mainly April-July.
dispersal_description: Seeds possibly spread by birds eating the fruits
ecology_description: Potential weed, garden escape. Seeds possibly spread by birds eating the fruits.
habitat_description: Disturbed areas near settlement, recorded from roadside, parkland, near walking tracks, riverbank, disturbed weedy eucalypt woodland, tall open Eucalyptus forest.
distribution_description: Occasionally naturalised in New South Wales in disturbed areas; localised adventive plants (sometimes with seedlings) have been recorded from SW Western Australia, Queensland (Brisbane area) and the Australian Capital Territory (Canberra area).

flowering_time_description: Flowers mainly (September-) November-December; fruits mainly April-July [parenthetical extremes]

common_name: Montane Tape Vine, Mountain Redberry Vine.
habit_description: Twining rambler or climber, glabrous except for the hair-tuft domatia and puberulous perianth
leaf_description: Leaves alternate, simple | lamina ovate to broadly ovate, 3--7.5 (-9) cm long, 1.8--5 cm wide, rounded or subcordate base, entire margin or frequently with 1 or 2 angles or lobes, gradually acute to acuminate apex, chartaceous (thin and soft), green above, paler and often whitish or greyish beneath, 3-veined in basal c. half, hairy domatia on undersurface in axils of midvein and the basal pair of lateral veins | petiole 1--3 cm long

distribution_description: Southeast Queensland to Barrington Tops area, New South Wales.
notes: For details on floral structure and development see Ronse de Craene (2017), who found floral development of Berberidopsis beckleri lies within a gradient from spiral flowers without perianth differentiation leading to flowers with differentiated sepals and petals.

common_name: Coast Redberry Vine, Coastal Redberry Vine.
flowering_time_description: Flowers recorded May, August, October, December
habit_description: Twining rambler or climber, glabrous
leaf_description: Leaves alternate, simple | lamina broadly ovate or ovate-elliptic to circular, 5--12 cm long, 3--10 (-12) cm wide, rounded to slightly cordate base, entire margin, acute to abruptly acuminate apex, rarely obtuse, subcoriaceous or soft, green both surfaces (glossy above, slightly paler and dull beneath), glabrous, 3-veined from base (basal pair of secondary veins often more prominent in basal c. half of lamina), domatia absent | petiole 2--7 cm long

phenology_text: Flowers recorded May, August, October, December.
habitat_description: Grows usually in subtropical rainforest and wet sclerophyll/tall open forest.
distribution_description: Southeast Queensland to Dorrigo area, New South Wales.

habit_description: Deciduous tree to 15 m high
leaf_description: Leaves | lamina ovate to suborbicular, 2--11 cm long, truncate or cordate at base, crenate, dentate or serrate margin, obtuse or acuminate apex, discolorous, glabrescent | petiole 2--3 cm long
fruit_description: Nutlet narrowly winged
habitat_description: Recorded from river banks.
distribution_description: Native of Italy and Corsica; recorded as sparingly naturalised near St Marys and New Norfolk in Tasmania by Curtis (1967: 645), however, a more recent assessment of specimens and recorded sites indicates that Alnus cordata is not naturalised in Tasmania (Baker et al. 2019: 34).

common_name: Black Alder, Common Alder, European Alder.
habitat_description: Beside streams, near lakes (often at edges) and damp ground, in disturbed landscapes and woodland; tolerant of water logged conditions.
distribution_description: Native of NW Europe, W Asia and N Africa. Naturalised in New South Wales (Katoomba) and the Australian Capital Territory (see Hosking et al. 2003: 179); doubtfully naturalised in Tasmania (Baker et al. 2019: 34).
notes: Possible naturalised records in the Australian Capital Territory are often associated with metropolitan parks near lake shores, including the environs of Lake Burley Griffin, and a disturbed stream beside Lake Ginninderra in Belconnen.

common_name: Trumpet Vine, Cow Itch, Trumpet Creeper, American Trumpet Vine.
leaflet_count_description: leaflets 7--11 (-13), with lamina ovate to narrowly ovate with an acute to drawn out pointed apex, to c. 8 cm long, discolorous
flowers_per_inflorescence_description: Flowers in clusters of up to 12
habit_description: Deciduous woody vine to scrambling shrub with aerial roots

notes: Specimens in New South Wales require further investigation to determine if they represent the hydrid Campsis ×tagliabuana.

common_name: Trumpet Creeper, Trumpet Vine, Hybrid Trumpet Vine.

distribution_description: Scattered records from south-western western Australia and central coast of New South Wales.
notes: Specimens of Campsis from New South Wales require further investigation to differentiate between Campsis radicans and Campsis ×tagliabuana.

common_name: Argentine Trumpet Vine, Violet Trumpet Vine, Painted Trumpet, Love Charm, Lavender Trumpet Vine.
flower_colour_description: pale lavender; mauve; violet; purple; yellowish
habit_description: Evergreen (to semi-deciduous) robust climber, woody-stemmed, climbing with tendrils
leaf_description: Leaves opposite, pinnate, often with a terminal simple tendril | leaflets usually 2 (sometimes a single leaflet) | lamina elliptic to obovate, mostly 5--9.5 cm long, 2--5 cm wide, glabrous | apex acute to acuminate | margin entire | undulate | petiole to 10 (-20) mm long, petiolules c. 2--7 mm long

habitat_description: In Eastwood in New South Wales recorded scattered along a creek in wet sclerophyll forest. Possible adventive plants also recorded near earlier plantings, old gardens and disturbed sites near settlement.

habit_description: Perennial woody climber, deciduous
leaf_description: Leaves opposite, usually 3-foliate | leaflets with lamina ovate to narrowly ovate, 20--40 mm or more long, glabrous except for hairs on margin and hairy domatia underleaf | apex acute to acumuinate | petiolules hairy above
inflorescence_description: Inflorescences terminal panicles
flower_description: Flowers showy, 5-merous | corolla tubular-funnelform, pink or purple-pink often with darker streaks and white throat (e.g. Cuspidaria convoluta 'Rosa Cipó'), or totally white (as in Cuspidaria convoluta 'Alba')

seed_description: seeds with translucent wing either side
distribution_description: Native from Bolivia to Brazil and NE Argentina (Plants of the World Online, accessed 9 August 2022). Reported as naturalised in New South Wales (Australian Plant Census, CHAH 2010, accessed 9 August 2022), however this record has not been substantiated to date.

common_name: Deplanchea, Golden Bouquet Tree, Wallaby Wireless Tree; Yellow Pagoda Flower Tree, Bignonia.
habit_description: See Zich et al. (2020)
ecology_description: One of the common names used for this species (Wallaby Wireless Tree) alludes to the fact that wallabies are fond of the fallen flowers of this species and once the flowers fall, the news seems to spread quickly throughout the wallaby population, who then assemble to partake of the apparently tasty fare.
habitat_description: Rainforest, beach forest, monsoon forest.
distribution_description: Cape York south to near Townsville, Queensland; also in New Guinea.

common_name: Cat's Claw Creeper, Cat's Claw Trumpet, Funnel Creeper.
habit_description: Vigorous woody climber, climbing by tripartite, hooked (uncinate) tendrils (resembling claws) and adventitious roots and tubers, glabrous
leaf_description: Leaves opposite, 3-foliate with the terminal leaflet modified into a 3-clawed tendril, each claw c. 10--15 mm long (tendrils absent from some leaves) | leaflets usually 2 (rarely 1 or 5 in juveniles), with lamina ovate to oblong-elliptic, 2--7 cm long, 10--30 (-35) mm wide, glabrous | apex acuminate | margin entire to obscurely toothed | petiole 10--20 cm long, petiolules (1.5-) 5--15 mm long
inflorescence_description: Panicles axillary, sometimes reduced to 1 or 3 flowers
flower_description: Flowers | calyx c. 10--15 (-20) mm long | corolla yellow often with darker or orangey lines in tube, 4--8 (-9) cm long | lobes to c. 2 cm long, white-ciliate margin | Stamens dimorphic, 2 long and 2 short and 1 staminode

ecology_description: Environmental weed that forms dense mats covering and outcompeting native vegetation. Cat’s Claw Creeper is listed as a Key Threatening Process in New South Wales because of its potential to impact on endangered and vulnerable plants as well as Lowland Subtropical Rainforest, which is an Endangered Ecological Community (see NSW WeedWise profile, accessed 9 August 2022).
habitat_description: Invasive weed in disturbed rainforest, sclerophyll forest, woodland, scrub and gallery forest/riparian vegetation, roadsides, often in gullies and creekbanks.
distribution_description: Native of Mexico through tropical America to Argentina (see Plants of the World Online, accessed 9 August 2022); in Australia naturalised chiefly in eastern Queensland and New South Wales from southern Cape York Peninsula south to the Sydney region.

habit_description: Shrubs or small trees (1.6-) 5--7 (-10) m high

habitat_description: Typically found in open woodland and on rocky hillsides on a variety of soil types.
distribution_description: Widespread in tropical Queensland from Torres Strait south to Charters Towers, 20°19' S, 146°46' E, west to 141° E and east to 146ᵒ 49' E.

fruiting_time_description: Flowering appears to range from September to December with fruiting specimens collected from April to November
habit_description: Erect shrub or small tree to 10 m high

phenology_text: Flowering appears to range from September to December with fruiting specimens collected from April to November.
habitat_description: Found in a variety of habitats from woodland to dune vegetation adjacent to mangroves.
distribution_description: Chiefly found on the eastern side of Cape York Peninsula from Thursday Island as far south as 18°45' S; common in the Weipa area, Queensland.

habit_description: Shrub or small tree to 4--5 (-9) m high
leaf_description: Leaves alternate to opposite, often clustered on short shoots | lamina linear-lanceolate to lanceolate even on same plant, 5--12 cm long, 0.4--2.5 (-2.6) cm wide | base markedly cuneate | apex acute to obtuse | lateral veins usually less than 15° to midrib | margins often wavy
phenology_text: The chief flowering period appears to be January to March, capsules commonly collected between March and July.
pollination_description: The presence of hawkmoths and the strong fragrance suggests the presence of a similar pollination system as mentioned by Frazão et al. (2020) and Mridula (2011)
ecology_description: Populations rarely more than 10 individuals and distance between populations is highly variable. Hawkmoths were observed visiting a number of plants in the Townsville area in the early evening. The presence of hawkmoths and the strong fragrance suggests the presence of a similar pollination system as mentioned by Frazão et al. (2020) and Mridula (2011).
habitat_description: Plants usually occur in open woodland on granitic soils.
distribution_description: This subspecies is found in open woodland and on margins of deciduous vine thickets south from c. 16° S on southern Cape York Peninsula to south of Charters Towers (20° 33' S), west from near Karumba to the Townsville area in the east, Queensland.

common_name: Mangrove Trumpet Tree, Tui, Trumpet Tree, vernacular names vary with country and area.

fruiting_time_description: In Australia, flowering occurs November-February, while fruits have been collected November-May

common_name: Golden Trumpet Tree, Yellow Trumpet Tree.

In Queensland (where the species is treated as doubtfully naturalised per Queensland Plant Census, accessed August 2022) adventive plants have been recorded near the Gold Coast, viz. northern edge of Brisbane Koala Bushlands, Alperton Rd, Burbank, M.J. Laidlaw 85, BRI (0.5--3 m tall seedlings in Eucalyptus open forest regrowth at road edge) and near Cairns, viz. Wongabel, Cairns railway corridor adjacent to Herberton Range State Forest, S.G. Mckenna 1967, CNS (disturbed weedy medium-open forest with note that "this species is colonising protected areas in parts of the Atherton Tablelands").

There is a record of unknown status from northern Queensland, viz. Lockhart River Rd, 6 km NW of Lockhart River town, J.J. Bruhl 1047, NE (in Eucalyptus woodland/Melaleuca).

An invasive environmental weed; see Spathodea campanulata Weeds of Australia fact sheet (accessed September 2022) and linked references.
habitat_description: Recorded, often as a garden escape in disturbed and weedy sites, from wet margin of a lake, banks of waterways, gullies, wetlands, rainforest, riverine forest/riparian vegetation, eucalypt woodland and open forest, roadsides; favours wetter habitats.
distribution_description: Native from western Tropical Africa to Uganda and Angola (Spathodea campanulata in Plants of the World Online, accessed 4 September 2022); naturalised in northern Australia in Western Australia, the Northern Territory and Queensland. Most records are from near coastal eastern Queensland. Naturalised and invading forests in many Pacific Islands, e.g. Vanuatu, Fiji, the Cook Islands, Hawaii.
notes: The fruit is poisonous.

common_name: Cape Honeysuckle, Fire Flower, Flame Vine, Red Tecoma, Tecoma.
habit_description: Evergreen, rambling, scrambling, scandent, subscandent or semi-erect shrub to 4 m high
leaf_description: Leaves imparipinnate, 6.5--14 cm long | leaflets usually 5--9, elliptic to ovate or circular to rhombic, 1--4 cm long, (5-) 10--25 mm wide, broad-cuneate to rounded base, serrated-toothed margin, acute to acuminate apex, glabrous, lateral petiolules 1--2 mm long | petiole 1--3 cm long
inflorescence_description: Inflorescences dense
flower_description: Calyx 3--6 mm long | Corolla 5--6 cm long, orange or reddish orange to scarlet, sometimes yellow (e.g. Tecoma capensis 'Aurea'), pubescent near base within tube and on lobe margins | tube curved, c. 3.5--4.5 cm long | lobes c. 10 mm long | Stamens exserted | anthers glabrous
fruit_description: Capsule linear-oblong, 3--7.5 cm long, c. 7 mm wide, winged seeds c. 15 mm long
dispersal_description: Spread by wind-dispersed winged seeds, root suckering and the dumping of garden waste
vegetative_reproduction_description: Spread by wind-dispersed winged seeds, root suckering and the dumping of garden waste
ecology_description: Spread by wind-dispersed winged seeds, root suckering and the dumping of garden waste. An environmental weed.
habitat_description: Recorded near settlement, roadsides, near waterways, wasteland, disturbed bushland, rainforest, coastal scrub.
distribution_description: Native of southern Africa. Naturalised in coastal districts in Western Australia, Queensland, New South Wales, Norfolk Island and Victoria. Possibly naturalised on Lord Howe Island where it has been recorded along a roadside as a garden escape.
notes: As observed by Green (1994) this species is commonly cultivated (including as a hedge plant) on Norfolk Island. de Lange et al. (2005) did not see any fruiting material on the island, but they noted that small prunings from hedge trimmings root freely, and presumably naturalisation on Norfolk Island resulted from the discarding of such material.

common_name: Yellow Bignonia, Yellow Trumpet Bush, Yellow Bells, Yellow Elder, Ginger-thomas, Yellow Trumpet Flowers, Tecoma.
habit_description: Shrub or sometimes small tree to 5 (-8+) m high
leaf_description: Leaves pinnate, 8--25 cm long | leaflets usually 3--7 but sometimes up to 13, ovate-lanceolate, 2.5--10 cm long, 8--30 (-35) mm wide, cuneate base, serrated-toothed margin, acuminate apex, glabrous (softly hairy below in var. velutina) | petiole 1--6 (-8) cm long, lateral petiolules 1--2 mm long
inflorescence_description: Inflorescences 5--15 cm long
flower_description: Calyx cupular to campanulate, 5--7 mm long, the 5 lobes c. 1 mm long | Corolla tubular to funnel-shaped, 3.5--5 cm long, bright yellow with reddish lines in throat which also has slight ridges with long hairs, the 5 rounded lobes 0.8--3 cm long, some cultivars, including hybrids, have orangy to reddish flowers | Stamens included
fruit_description: Capsules pendulous, linear-oblong, somewhat flattened, 7--22 (-30) cm long, (5-) 9--20 mm wide, winged seeds flat, c. 20 mm long and 6 mm wide (including wing surrounding oblong-oval shaped seed) | the wing at each end of the seed white-transparent, papery
dispersal_description: The winged seeds are dispersed mainly by wind and water It has also been spread by the dumping of garden waste
fire_response_description: Tecoma stans can regenerate from cut roots and by suckering, especially when disturbed
vegetative_reproduction_description: Tecoma stans can regenerate from cut roots and by suckering, especially when disturbed
ecology_description: Garden escape; potential invasive weed. The winged seeds are dispersed mainly by wind and water. Tecoma stans can regenerate from cut roots and by suckering, especially when disturbed. It has also been spread by the dumping of garden waste.
habitat_description: Disturbed sites, near settlement and gardens, recorded from roadsides, rail corridors, parkland, agricultural land, wasteland, open eucalypt forest, woodland, bushland gullies, grassland, rainforest, river banks/riparian areas, wetland, beach habitats/sand dunes.
distribution_description: Native of southern U.S.A., Mexico, Peru and Ecuador. In Australia a garden escape and naturalised, mainly in coastal districts, in Western Australia, on Christmas Island, in Queensland (from Torres Strait islands to SE Qld) and New South Wales. There also appear to be adventive records from the Northern Territory.
notes: A treatment for Tecoma stans on Christmas Island is provided by Barker (1993).

leaflet_count_description: Leaves opposite, trifoliolate or pinnate, and occasional leaflets bearing lobes or pinnules
habit_description: Canopy climber to 30 m
stem_description: branchlets to 3 cm diam., terete, often twisted, with sparse globular pale lenticels, glabrescent to glabrous except at leaf nodes where puberulous along a raised interpetiolar ridge
leaf_description: Leaves opposite, trifoliolate or pinnate, and occasional leaflets bearing lobes or pinnules | petiole 20--70 mm long | leaflets usually 3--5, fleshy, discolorous | midvein slightly depressed on the adaxial surface and strongly raised on abaxial surface | 4--6 pairs of main lateral veins, strongly raised on abaxial surface | venation brochidodromous | tertiary veins usually scarcely discernible | lateral leaflets ovate, elliptic to lanceolate, (40-) 55--97 (-110) mm long, 15--42 mm wide | base obtuse to cuneate or truncate | oblique | margin entire to sparsely toothed distally | often undulate | apex acute to acuminate | abaxial surface minutely puberulous and finely punctate glandular, petiolule (0-) 2--11 mm long, grooved on upper surface | terminal leaflet ovate, elliptic to lanceolate, 58--112 mm long, 20--52 mm wide | base obtuse to cuneate | sometimes oblique | margin entire to sparsely toothed distally | often undulate | apex acute to acuminate | abaxial surface minutely puberulous and finely punctate glandular, petiolule 7--25 mm long, grooved on upper surface
inflorescence_description: peduncle short | bracts lanceolate to linear, c. 0.2--1.9 mm long | rachis 3--24 mm long, linear bracts subtending flowers 3--6 mm long | pedicels 6--19 mm | bracteoles 2.5--4.8 mm long, linear, paired near base of pedicel | pedicel persistent, 15--17.6 mm long
flower_description: Flowers opposite, 2 per node | Calyx infundibuliform (trumpet-shaped), with 5 equal lobes, 5 midribs prominent from base of the calyx to the tip of the lobes on the adaxial surface, thin and herbaceous, 22--36 mm long from base to tip of lobes, pale green to pink-tinged | lobes erect, ovate-triangular, 6.5--12 mm long, 5--10 mm wide, shortly hairy near apex | apex cuspidate | Corolla 58--86 mm long, infundibuliform, asymmetrical, curved, pale to dark pink, paler at the base | throat cream to pale pink and darkening with age, with purple striations | lobes 5, 12--14 mm long, 12--14 mm wide | apex bluntly pointed | tube 55--73 mm long, 24--33 mm diam., glabrous outside, glabrous to sparsely hairy inside, glandular papillae and sometimes uniseriate hairs near insertion of stamens | lobes shortly hairy on both surfaces | Stamens 4, not exserted, curved, fused to corolla for 15--19 mm from base, 2 pairs of slightly unequal length, abaxial pair 37--43 mm, adaxial pair 30--35 mm, glabrous except near base where shortly uniseriate hairs present or absent, and glandular papillose hairs present | filaments filiform | anthers yellow, cells equal, 5--6 mm long, 2.5--3 mm wide, widely divergent | Staminode adaxial, fused to corolla for 16--25 mm from base, free length 14--20 (-23) mm | apex curved | at base with uniseriate hairs | Style longer than stamens, included, 56--64 mm long | stigmas 2, sublanceolate | Ovary compressed, 2.4--5 mm long, 2.5 mm wide, glabrous | calyx persistent
fruit_description: Capsule stipitate and beaked capsule, 138--180 mm long (from base of stipe), c. 33 mm wide | valves smooth, woody, wide and boat shaped
seed_description: seeds numerous, orbicular and notched, 3.7 × 4.3 mm, with membranous wings 27 mm long × 12.7 mm wide
habitat_description: Grows in lowland, upland and mountain rainforest.
distribution_description: Endemic to Wet Tropics bioregion in northeastern Queensland, from the Big Tableland area south of Cooktown to the Mount Windsor Tableland, Daintree National Park area, north from the Daintree River.

common_name: Pink Trumpet Vine, Fraser Island Creeper.
habit_description: Climber, twining
leaf_description: Leaves opposite, usually 5-foliate | leaflets ovate to lanceolate or elliptic-ovate, to 8 cm long and 3 cm wide
inflorescence_description: Racemes
flower_description: Flowers rich pink, paler on inside with dark stripes, to 8 cm long
fruit_description: Pod to 6 cm long
habitat_description: Rainforest, swampy open forest.
distribution_description: Coastal areas between Fraser Island and Bli Bli, south-eastern Queensland.

habit_description: Tree to 8 m high
leaf_description: Leaves ovate, acuminate | lamina 7--24 cm long, 4--16 cm wide, cordate at base, red-dotted, lepidote beneath when young, lateral nerves prominent beneath, connected by many parallel nerves | petiole 4.5--12 cm long | stipules 6--10 mm long
inflorescence_description: Pedicels 8--10 mm long | the apex with sessile glands alternating with sepals
flower_description: Flowers 4--6 cm diam | Sepals obovate, obtuse, 10--12 mm long, concave, densely lepidote | Petals 5--7, obovate, unequal, 2--3 cm long, pink or white, dotted outside | Anthers violet | Ovary densely setose
fruit_description: Capsule ovoid, obtuse or acute, c. 5 cm long, covered with red bristles
seed_description: Seeds 4--5 mm long
distribution_description: Native to central America and the West Indies; naturalised in Queensland.
notes: The orange dye annatto, obtained from the seeds, still used in some countries to colour butter and cheese, and by some peoples in P.N.G. to dye hair and skin.

habit_description: Shrub or tree to 6 m
leaf_description: Leaves 3--7-lobed up to ½ length, glabrous or velvety | lamina mostly 5--10 cm long, 7--15 cm wide, cordate at base | lobes ovate, often broad and shallow, rounded, crenate to almost entire | petiole 6--13 cm long | stipules 1--2 mm long
inflorescence_description: Inflorescence up to 30 cm long | bracts scale-like
flower_description: Flowers 5.5--8 cm diam | Sepals ovate, strigose to glabrous, the outer 7--10 mm long, 4--7 mm wide, the inner 10--16 mm long, 6--15 mm wide | Petals 3--4 cm long | Staminal filaments yellow | anthers 2--3.5 mm long, basal pores small or none
fruit_description: Capsule ovoid, 5.5--8 cm long
distribution_description: Occurs in N Australia from the Kimberley to Arnhem Land.
notes: There are two subspecies.

leaf_description: Leaves glabrous, rarely pubescent | the margins glabrous
inflorescence_description: Bracts 2 mm long
habitat_description: Grows in sand or among sandstone rocks, in eucalypt woodland, rarely in shallow depressions.
distribution_description: Occurs in N.T. north of Katherine.

leaf_description: Leaves pubescent, rarely glabrous | the margins velvety
inflorescence_description: Bracts 4.5--8 mm long
habitat_description: Grows in a wide range of soils, usually in open woodland.
distribution_description: Occurs from the NW Kimberley, W.A., to Katherine, N.T.

habit_description: Shrub or small tree to 10 m high
leaf_description: Leaves 5--7-lobed, glabrous | lamina 5--15 cm long, 7--18 cm wide, cordate at base | lobes lanceolate to narrowly obovate, acute | margins serrate | often obscurely so | petiole 6--15 cm long | stipules 3.5--4 cm long
inflorescence_description: Inflorescence up to 12 cm long | bracts scale-like
flower_description: Flowers 7--10 cm diam | Sepals ovate, minutely strigose to glabrous, the outer 8--11 mm long, 4--7 mm wide, the inner 10--13 mm long, 8--12 mm wide | Petals 3.5--4 cm long, 2--2.5 cm wide | Staminal filaments red | anthers 3--4 mm long
fruit_description: Capsule obovoid, 6--9.5 cm long
habitat_description: Grows in sand, on sandstone and granite, in eucalypt woodland, sometimes on creek banks.
distribution_description: Occurs in NE Arnhem Land, N.T., and NE Qld from Cape York to Townsville. Also in P.N.G.

habitat_description: Grows in sand, sandstone and laterite, in open woodland.
distribution_description: Occurs in N.T. and Qld near the Gulf of Carpentaria.

leaf_description: Leaves to c. 1 m long | lamina flat with veins and midrib slightly raised, 4--12 mm wide | margins hyaline and slightly revolute | smooth
inflorescence_description: Inflorescence a contracted umbel-like raceme, to c. 0.8 m long, 12--30-flowered | peduncle to c. 8 mm diam. | pedicels to c. 4.5 cm long, about as long as to much exceeding subtending bract
flower_description: Perianth usually 3--6 cm long, red with yellow lobes | tube narrowly cylindrical in lower quarter to third but expanded abruptly and bell-shaped upwards, 2--3 cm wide at throat | lobes ovate, acute, to 12 mm long | Filaments to c. 3.5 cm long, attached below middle of perianth tube | anthers oblong or tapered slightly upwards, 3.8--5 mm long
fruit_description: Capsule to c. 9 cm long including style | stipe to c. 4 cm long
habitat_description: Found in damp shallow sandy and peaty soils, often on cliff edges.
distribution_description: Occurs in the Blue Mountains, N.S.W.
notes: G. Bentham's Blandfordia grandiflora var. elongata may represent a hybrid between this species and B. grandiflora. Blandfordia ×flammea-elegans W.G.Sm., Floral Mag. n. ser. t. 134 (1874), was claimed by the author to apply to a hybrid between B. cunninghamii and B. flammea (= B. grandiflora ). No origin was given for the material concerned, and apparently no specimen of it has been preserved.

flowering_time_description: Flowers late spring and early summer
leaf_description: Leaves to c. 70 cm long | lamina folded or flat, channelled, keeled, 2--5 mm wide | margins somewhat thickened but flat or inrolled | crenulate-scabrid
inflorescence_description: Inflorescence loosely racemose, to c. 1.75 m long, usually 3--9-flowered | peduncle to c. 7 mm diam. | pedicels to 4.5 cm long, as long as to much longer than subtending bract
flower_description: Perianth usually 3.5--6 cm long, red with yellow lobes or wholly yellow, with a slight bloom | tube turbinate, gradually expanded upwards with slight shoulder in lower third, 1.8--3 cm wide at throat | lobes semicircular but tips ultimately acute, to c. 12 mm long | Filaments to c. 3 cm long, attached from slightly below middle to towards base of tube | anthers oblong, 3--4.5 mm long
fruit_description: Capsule to c. 6 cm long including style | stipe to c. 6 cm long
phenology_text: Flowers late spring and early summer.
habitat_description: Occurs in damp sandy and/or peaty soils.
distribution_description: Extends from coastal and tableland areas in north-eastern N.S.W. to near-coastal areas E of Gympie in south-eastern Qld.
notes: Forms (possibly hybrid) approaching Blandfordia nobilis may be encountered in the southern portions of its range. B. intermedia Herb. is apparently applicable to one of these. Forms approaching B. cunninghamii (I.Bowden , NSW 109401) in the Blue Mountains possibly represent hybrids with that species. In addition, abnormal forms with more than 15 apparently sterile flowers up to 6 cm long, pedicels up to 9 cm long and leaf-like bracts up to 20 cm long have been observed near Caloundra (Qld) and Bulahdelah (N.S.W.). No taxonomic importance is given here to these latter forms as they appear insect- or virus-affected.

leaf_description: Leaves to c. 60 cm long | lamina channelled, keeled, c. 5 mm wide | margins straight and slightly thickened | crenulate-scabrid or smooth
inflorescence_description: Inflorescence loosely racemose, to c. 0.75 m long, 3--20-flowered | peduncle to c. 4 mm diam. | pedicels to 3 cm long, much longer than subtending bract
flower_description: Perianth usually 2--3 cm long, brownish red with yellow lobes | tube narrowed in lower 1/3, expanded and cylindrical above, to c. 1 cm wide at throat | lobes ovate, obtuse but apiculate, c. 5 mm long | Filaments 1.5--2 cm long, attached just below middle of perianth tube | anthers oblong, 2--2.8 mm long
fruit_description: Capsule to c. 6 cm long including style | stipe to c. 2.5 cm long
habitat_description: Grows in swampy areas.
distribution_description: Occurs in N.S.W. from the central coast inland to the Blue Mts, and in the southern coast and tablelands districts.
notes: A moderately variable species with extremes approaching Blandfordia grandiflora in the northern parts of its range, suggesting the two species may hybridise there.

leaf_description: Leaves to c. 35 cm long, upper conspicuously shorter than lower | lamina flat, channelled, keeled, 4--12 mm wide | margins straight | slightly thickened, crenulate
inflorescence_description: Inflorescence shortly racemose, to c. 1 m long, 15--50-flowered | peduncle to c. 6 mm diam. | pedicels to 6.5 cm long, usually much longer than subtending bract
flower_description: Perianth usually 3.5--4.5 cm long, red-brown abaxially, yellow adaxially | tube narrowly conical, 1.5--2 cm wide at throat | lobes ovate, ultimately acute, to c. 8 mm long | the margins yellow abaxially | Filaments 0.8--1.1 cm long, attached conspicuously above middle of tube | anthers oblong, 3.5--4 mm long
fruit_description: Capsule to c. 5.5 cm long including style | stipe to c. 4 cm long
habitat_description: Locally abundant on damp sandy and acid heaths and moors.
distribution_description: Occurs in Tas., from lower altitudes in the north-east, south-east and high mountainous regions of the west.

leaf_description: Fronds similar or dimorphic, pendulous, 7--50 (-114) cm long, 3--15 (-27) cm wide | Stipe 3--15 (-47) cm long, stramineous to brown, purplish at base | scales narrowly lanceolate to ovate, acuminate, entire to finely dentate, brown to red-brown | Lamina deltoid to ovate, pinnate, with 5--14 pairs of pinnae | sterile pinnae oblong-lanceolate to ovate, 1.5--14 cm long, 8--29 mm wide, shortly stalked at base of lamina, partly adnate at apex | margins serrate | basal pinnae similar or slightly shorter | fertile pinnae irregular in width
inflorescence_description: rachis and costae stramineous | scales acuminate to subulate, often finely dentate, brown to red-brown, sometimes with lanuginose hairs
habitat_description: Grows in soil pockets, often on rock faces and ledges in moist areas and sometimes in rainforest and wet sclerophyll forest.
distribution_description: Endemic and intermittent in coastal and tableland regions on the eastern coast, from central Qld to the south coast of N.S.W.

underground_organ_description: Rhizome sometimes forming a short erect trunk
leaf_description: Fronds dimorphic, 12--50 (-165) cm long, 4--25 (-80) cm wide | Stipe 4--82 cm long, stramineous to reddish brown, glabrous except for narrow triangular acuminate entire dark reddish brown scales at base | Lamina ovate, pinnate, with 5--20 pairs of pinnae | sterile pinnae narrowly lanceolate, tapering to both ends, 2.5--36 cm long, 10--25 mm wide, stalked at base of lamina, becoming sessile towards apex, stalk articulated at rachis | margins entire | crenate to serrate at apices | basal pinnae similar or slightly shorter | fertile pinnae linear, 6--27 cm long, 1.5--6 mm wide
inflorescence_description: rachis and costae stramineous to reddish brown, glabrous
habitat_description: Grows along wet stream banks in rainforest.
distribution_description: Endemic to mountain ranges of north-eastern Qld.

underground_organ_description: Rhizome creeping, erect trunk to 50 (-150) cm high
leaf_description: Fronds dimorphic, 45--100 (-150) cm long, 4--30 cm wide | Stipe 12--60 cm long, purplish black, brown to reddish brown, basal scales linear-lanceolate, acuminate, entire, brown to reddish brown or bicolorous, scale scars present above | Lamina ovate to lanceolate, pinnate, with 6--37 pairs of pinnae | sterile pinnae oblong-lanceolate, acuminate, auriculate-hastate (especially basiscopically), 7--25 cm long, 8--20 mm wide, shortly stalked at base of lamina, adnate towards apex | margins serrate | basal pinnae gradually reduced and more widely spaced | fertile pinnae 7--17 cm long, 3--5 mm wide
inflorescence_description: rachis and costae stramineous or concolorous with stipe | scales reddish brown (sometimes bicolorous and often with dentate bases) | fine scale and hair material often persistent in grooves
habitat_description: Grows in low-lying swampy land, usually in coastal habitats.
distribution_description: Endemic to south-eastern Qld and in northern and central coastal regions of N.S.W.

leaf_description: Stipe 8--70 cm long, brown to stramineous, blackening at base, basal scales subulate, entire, black, scale scars above | Lamina deltoid to ovate, pinnate, with 12--25 (-50) pairs of pinnae | sterile pinnae linear-lanceolate, 2--19 cm long, 6--15 mm wide, acuminate, adnate or semi-adnate throughout with broad bases with margins serrate | basal pinnae similar or longer and deflexed | fertile pinnae similar or slightly narrower
inflorescence_description: rachis and costae stramineous to brown, glabrous or with sparse scales and hairs
habitat_description: Common but intermittent in a broad range of plant communities and a variety of substrata, from sea-level to 1000 m, occasionally in forest margins or moist open heaths in montane areas. In drier regions it is confined to gullies and stream banks in sclerophyllous forest.
distribution_description: Endemic to eastern and south-eastern Australia, from northern Qld to Vic.; no reliable records for Tas.

leaf_description: Fronds dimorphic, 12--65 cm long, 2--10 cm wide | Stipe 2--15 cm long, stramineous, becoming purplish black towards the base | scales linear-lanceolate, subulate, broadly based, entire, reddish brown | Lamina narrowly linear-lanceolate, pinnate, with 17--40 or more pairs of pinnae | Sterile pinnae oblong, falcate, obtuse to acuminate, 1.5--3.2 cm long, 5--10 mm wide, adnate with broad bases | margins crenate to serrate | basal pinnae shorter and more obtuse | Fertile pinnae linear, 1.2--4.5 cm long, 1--2.5 mm wide, reduced and often sterile towards lamina base
inflorescence_description: Rachis and costae stramineous, often dark purplish towards base on undersurface, glabrous or with very sparse short acuminate reddish brown scales
habitat_description: Grows in areas of constant high humidity, such as gullies, stream banks and cave entrances, often found in the spray zone of waterfalls.
distribution_description: Known in south-eastern S.A., south-western and eastern N.S.W., southern Vic. and Tas.; widespread in New Zealand, and extends to some Pacific islands.

habit_description: Climbing epiphyte fern
underground_organ_description: Rhizome long, covered with dense, narrowly lanceolate scales | scales c. 1.5 cm long, with a long fine apex
leaf_description: Fronds dimorphic, 0.5--2 cm apart on rhizome | stipe 5--10 cm long, with a few scattered, narrow scales | Sterile fronds erect, not geniculate | lamina pinnate, overall outline narrowly lanceolate, 30--50 cm or more long, 5--12 cm broad, glabrous or a few narrow scales beside midrib beneath | base with gradually reduced pinnae | pinnae 30--40 pairs, borne at an angle of 45°-60° to midrib, not overlapping, narrowly elongate-triangular, sometimes somewhat falcate, (2.5-) 3--7 cm long, 0.5--1 cm broad at base, diminishing gradually to a long-acute apex, with bases entire | veins distinct below | usually forked once | Lamina of fertile fronds pinnate | pinnae 40--50 pairs, narrowly linear, 4--10 cm long
habitat_description: Frequent in the cloud-forest on the summits of Mts Gower and Lidgbird.
distribution_description: Occurs on Lord Howe Island; also known from New Caledonia.
notes: The New Caledonian plants tend to be larger and bear pinnae which are more parallel sided.

underground_organ_description: Rhizome creeping to erect, often forming a short trunk
leaf_description: Fronds dimorphic, 10--68 cm long, 3--10 cm wide | Stipe 9--36 cm long, stramineous to brown | scales linear to narrowly triangular, acuminate, entire, dark reddish brown, with straight white hairs at least at base of stipe | Lamina narrowly triangular, pinnatisect or pinnate, with 6--30 or more pairs of pinnae | sterile pinnae oblong to narrowly triangular, often slightly falcate, acuminate, 3.2--8 cm long, 8--10 mm wide, sometimes pilose, fully adnate | margins crenate | basal pinnae broader, more falcate, markedly deflexed and not adnate basiscopically | fertile pinnae 3--4.5 cm long, 2--3.5 mm wide
inflorescence_description: rachis and costae stramineous to brown, glabrous in Australian material
habitat_description: Grows in a wide range of cool moist situations, e.g. forests and exposed grasslands.
distribution_description: Occurs in upland areas of Vic. and in lowland to mountainous areas of Tas.; also in New Zealand.
notes: Despite an extensive geographic range this taxon is often rare. The Tasmanian populations tend to be more sparsely pilose than those from New Zealand (and most Pacific and Indonesian material re Blechnum vulcanicum s. lat.).

leaf_description: Stipe without tubercles | Fronds dimorphic | Lamina pinnate, 6--31 cm long, 4--70 mm wide, apical lobe c. one-quarter to one-seventh of lamina length | Pinnae simple or at least some lobed to pinna midvein | lobes 1--3 pairs | pinnae in basal and middle parts of frond stalked, those in distal part decurrent on basiscopic side, longest fertile pinnae 2--60 mm long, 1--6 mm wide
inflorescence_description: rachis and pinna midvein without tubercles
habitat_description: Lithophytic in crevices in open notophyll vine forest and Eucalyptus forest.
distribution_description: Endemic to eastern Qld.

leaf_description: Stipe without tubercles | Fronds dimorphic | Lamina 12.5--39 cm long, 0.7--11 cm wide, apical lobe c. (one-third-) one-sixth to one-ninth of lamina length, deeply pinnatifid almost throughout | Pinnae simple, basal pair of pinna sometimes free, 2 or 3 more distal pairs adnate or decurrent, others decurrent to wing along rachis, longest fertile pinnae 4--87 mm long, 1.5--3 mm wide
inflorescence_description: rachis and pinna midvein without tubercles
habitat_description: Found in rainforest and wet sclerophyll forest, often growing in rock crevices on cliff faces or by streams.
distribution_description: Endemic to south-eastern Qld.

underground_organ_description: Rhizome creeping or a short erect trunk
leaf_description: Fronds dimorphic, (fertile fronds more erect), 10Chambers & Farrant (1998; 367)75 cm long, 1.5--7 cm wide (1--3 cm for fertile fronds) | Stipe usually less than 5 cm long, stramineous, reddish or dark brown | scales acuminate, entire, brown to reddish brown | Lamina oblong-lanceolate, pinnate, with 12--50 or more pairs of pinnae | sterile pinnae rounded to oblong, obtuse, 8--37 mm long, 4--12 mm wide, shortly stalked at base of lamina, becoming increasingly adnate towards apex | margins usually crenate | basal pinnae shorter and rounder | fertile pinnae 7--22 mm long, 1.5--3.5 mm wide
inflorescence_description: rachis and costae stramineous to reddish brown, with small brown scales and short whitish hairs
habitat_description: Grows in cool shady moist situations such as forested gullies, stream banks and near waterfalls.
distribution_description: Occurs in eastern and south-eastern N.S.W., A.C.T., southern Vic. and Tas.; also in New Zealand, the mountains of New Guinea, Indonesia and Malaysia.

habit_description: Terrestrial or lithophytic fern
underground_organ_description: Rhizome prominent, apical scales narrow, twisted, c. 1.5 cm long, long-pointed
leaf_description: Fronds dimorphic, clustered | stipe 5--10 cm long, with dense setose hairs and narrow scales, especially towards base | Lamina of sterile fronds pinnate or deeply pinnatifid, elliptic in outline, 30--50 cm long, 8--14 cm broad, with dense, dark brown, setose hairs on rachis and costae, scattered below | pinnae 15--25 pairs, entire, blunt at apex, often contiguous or sometimes overlapping slightly, longest pinnae 5--7 cm long, 1.2--2 cm broad in the middle | basal pinnae gradually reduced in length | veins mostly forked twice | pinnae in lower half of frond auriculate | upper pinnae adnate | Lamina of fertile fronds pinnate | pinnae 15--20 pairs, linear, 3--6 cm long
habitat_description: Cloud forest.
distribution_description: Endemic to Lord Howe Island where confined to the cloud-forest on the top of Mt Gower.

leaflet_count_pairs_description: pinnae 15--25 pairs, entire, blunt at apex, often contiguous or sometimes overlapping slightly, longest pinnae 5--7 cm long, 1.2--2 cm broad in the middle

habitat_description: Usually on creek banks in rainforests; a species tolerant of deep shade.
distribution_description: Endemic. Occurs in south-eastern Qld, eastern N.S.W., A.C.T., southern Vic. and northern Tas. Also on Lord Howe Is.
notes: Habit may vary from plant to plant in a single population, and fronds may vary from simple to dissected, even on the same plant. Variation has proved inconsistent and random in cultivation, except that well-established vigorously growing plants, once they have started to produce dissected fronds, continue to do so unless conditions for growth alter dramatically. However, under the same conditions of growth, plants grown side by side and originally from the same population may continue producing only simple fronds indefinitely. More robust fleshy-fronded plants from north-eastern Qld, formerly assigned to B. patersonii, are now recognised as subspecies queenslandicum. Only the latter occurs in northern Qld, but both are found in south-eastern Qld and north-eastern N.S.W. Subsp. patersonii is less robust with more wiry paler stipe and rachis, and has thin papery fronds with undulate crenate to serrate margins; subsp. queenslandicum is fleshy and brittle when fresh, coriaceous when pressed, with stouter more pigmented stipes, and the margins of the lamina including the wings down the rachis are thin, smooth and entire.

distribution_description: Occurs in eastern Qld and north-eastern N.S.W., with the most distinct and robust forms being found in northern Qld; extends to the Milne Bay district of Papua New Guinea.

There has been considerable taxonomic confusion between B. patersonii, the New Zealand species B. colensoi (Hook.f.) N.A.Wakef. and an undescribed species occurring from Sri Lanka to Vanuatu. The latter two are thick, fleshy and brittle (like subsp. queenslandicum), but they have auricles rather than wings.

ecology_description: Hardy shoreline species. Tolerates saline conditions, nutrient-poor sands and rocky soils, and exposed seaward conditions. Has drift seeds, the corky mesocarp of the fruit adapts the species for water dispersal. Ecological role in coastal stabilisation (wind break from salt spray, sand-binding properties, e.g. dune stabilisation) and faunal habitat. Faunal habitat properties of the plant are described by Pike & Leach (1997: 30), e.g. leaf litter habitat for Hermit Crabs, food and shelter for insects, nesting sites for birds and turtles.
habitat_description: Coastal habitats, including exposed seaward side of coastal sand and coral debris dunes, coral cays, strand areas, flats above beaches, headlands, in littoral rainforest, vine thickets, beach forest, Casuarina woodland, littoral open scrub, strand vegetation, coral shingle with Pandanus. On Christmas Island D.A. Powell recorded Argusia argentea as occurring only in the spray zone among Scaevola taccada and Pemphis acidula but it appears to occur around the whole island in strand forest with Hibiscus tiliaceus and Cordia subcordata at beach tops or on low sea cliffs. Common on Cocos (Keeling) Islands on both atolls in strand communities on ocean and lagoon beach tops with Scaevola taccada, Calophyllum inophyllum and Cocos nucifera in calcareous sand. On Ashmore Reef recorded on strand line of West Island, as scattered on Middle Island and as one occurrence on East Island, by J. Hicks, ANPWS, pers. comm. On the Coral Sea Islands recorded for Herald Cays, Diamond Island, Coringa Island, Magdelaine Cays, Willis Island and Cato Island, usually dominant in leeward shrub communities in coralline sand.

habit_description: Biennial or perennial herb, erect, to 1 m high, branched

habit_description: Biennial or perennial, woody at base, usually glabrous, often glaucescent, erect, to 50 cm high

habit_description: Annual herb

common_name: Turnip, Long Black Turnip, Wild Turnip, White Turnip, Rapeseed, Turnip, Rape.

habit_description: Annual herb
stem_description: stem to 60 cm high, branching, hispid at base to glabrous above

common_name: Indian Mustard, Leaf Mustard, Brown Mustard, Chinese Mustard.

common_name: Oilseed Rape, Rapeseed, Rape, Canola, Swede.

profile_author: H.J. Hewson, P.S. Green, P.G. Kodela
habit_description: Succulent herb to 60 cm high, decumbent, branched from base

notes: Although recorded from Norfolk Island by J.H. Maiden, Proceedings of the Linnean Society of New South Wales 28: 695 (1904), no material from there has been seen, and R.M. Laing, Transactions and Proceedings of the Royal Society of New Zealand 47: 27 (1915), commented that it was 'almost certainly introduced and adventive'. It is quite possible that seed of this species could from time to time wash up on the shore, germinate and flower, yet not persist.

common_name: Sea Rocket, European Sea Rocket, Two-horned Sea Rocket.
habit_description: Annual herb, with ascending or decumbent branches to 80 cm long

There are several collections recorded for Lord Howe Island: Neds Beach, B.J. Conn 4287 (BRI, MEL, NSW), Neds Beach, near shed, J.M. Le Cussan 867 (BRI, NSW); Old Settlement Beach, Swarbrick 10492 (BRI), fide Australasian Virtual Herbarium (accessed 23 February 2026).

habit_description: Erect herb to 80 cm high, not or sparingly branched, somewhat hairy

habit_description: Perennial herb, glabrous
stem_description: Vegetative stems long, growing horizontally, rooting at nodes, occasionally branching, turning upwards to produce an erect, usually unbranched flowering stem to c. 25 cm high
leaf_description: Leaves somewhat fleshy | basal leaves long-petiolate, simple or pinnate with 1 or 2 pinna pairs and a larger terminal pinna, to c. 15 cm long, mostly arising singly along vegetative stem, sometimes several clustered at base of flowering stem | terminal pinna ovate to elliptic, cuneate to cordate at the base | lateral pinnae orbicular to elliptic | cauline leaves usually several, pinnate to pinnatisect, the lateral lobes/pinnae angled strongly forwards

Areas include Barrington Tops National Park in the Northern Tablelands of N.S.W., the Southern Tablelands of N.S.W., several localities in the Alpine region of Victoria, notably Falls Creek and Mt Hotham areas, and from near Cradle Mountain in Tasmania.

habit_description: Annual herb, rarely perennial in Australia, to 50 cm high, erect, occasionally decumbent and rooting at nodes (Thompson 1996b; 437), sparsely hirsute

In 2001, surveys found Lepidium peregrinum occurs in scattered refugia in northeastern New South Wales (near Tenterfield) and southeastern Queensland; see N.S.W. Office of Environment & Heritage (accessed February 2021) for details: https://www.environment.nsw.gov.au/threatenedspeciesapp/profile.aspxid=10464 Lepidium peregrinum was previously recorded from the Great Dividing Range, from the Blue Mountains and northeastern New South Wales.

For a history of the species from its first discovery in the United Kingdom to its connection of origin in Australia, then being presumed extinct and later rediscovered see Scarlett (1999). It is suggested that a sole occurrence of the plant in New Zealand found in 2010 results from the importing of goods directly from Sydney, New South Wales, to Kawhia by Maori during the 1830s to 1860s (Heenan & de Lange 2011). For a more detailed description, notes on leaf form, inflorescences and siliculae, habitat, and diagnostic characters of Lepidium peregrinum and closely related species, see Scarlett (1999).

The plant reproduces by lateral shoots from the base, from the apex of the rachis below the synangium, and from the tuft of sterile leaves at the apex of the synangium. The plant is probably established over most of its cultivated range, but because of its method of propagation has not spread. The naturalised population near Innisfail does not resemble any common commercial cultivar and may represent a reversion to the 'ancestral' form.

ecology_description: The senior author observed populations near Brisbane for about 5 years and during that time had not seen any mature fruit. No mature fruits were seen on any of the herbarium specimens examined. Ørgaard (1991: 199) observed that seed set in this species is much reduced in its native range as well, and ascribed this to reduced pollen fertility and possibly reduced stigma receptivity, consequent on its high polyploid chromosome number. Australian populations apparently reproduce vegetatively only, by fragmentation of the brittle stems and rhizomes. For details on life cycle, origin and distribution, habitat, dispersal and other properties of this species see Parsons & Cuthbertson (2001: 353--354). The mealy bug Hypogeococcus festerianus, which was introduced as a biological control for Harrisia martinii, provides a degree of control (Queensland Government 2016).

flower_description: Flowers subterminal, 20--35 mm diam | Perianth lobes firm, erect | outer tepals red, succulent, oblong, forming a firm cap in bud stage, 6--12 mm long, 2--5 mm wide | inner tepals dull red, oblong to oblanceolate, 10--15 mm long, 4--7 mm wide | Filament reddish above, white below | anthers pale yellow | Style white to pale pink-purple | stigma green
fruit_description: Fruit ellipsoid to oblong-urceolate, 3--7 cm long, 2--4 cm diam., with deep apical depression when young, tuberculate, yellowish green to orange when ripe, often persisting, sometimes proliferating, areoles on pericarpel often with a few weak deciduous spines
seed_description: Seeds 4--6 mm diam
habitat_description: A weed of roadsides and tracks, abandoned homesteads, and margins of natural vegetation (e.g. mallee, dry open Eucalyptus forest), usually in drier regions. A common weed in South Australia, occasional in Victoria, but rare in Western Australia and New South Wales.
distribution_description: There is some uncertainty regarding the natural range of the species. In the protologue of the species, Lamarck cited Peru as the origin, but other authors cited Chile as the natural range. Britton and Rose (1937) noted that the species was abundant in Ecuador but not found in either Peru or Chile. Anderson (2001) gives the origin as the central highlands of Ecuador. The species is classified as Near Threatened on the IUCN Red List (Loiza 2017), which provides a distribution map showing a large area in central Ecuador, with a localised disjunct occurrence in far northern Peru. Naturalised occasionally in New South Wales and Victoria as a garden escape.

flower_description: Flowers subterminal, 45--60 mm long, 30--35 mm diam | Perianth lobes firm, erect or slightly spreading | outer tepals green with pink fringe or pink, succulent, oblong to triangular, 4--15 mm long, 4--7 mm wide | inner tepals pink, oblanceolate | the apex obtuse | 22--25 mm long, 4--7 mm wide | Filaments white below | anthers pale yellow | Style white to pale pink | stigmas pale yellow
fruit_description: Fruit elongate, obovoid-oblong to clavate or globose, 50--130 mm long, 25--50 mm diam., tuberculate, green, often persisting, solitary or sometimes proliferating, areoles with or without spines
seed_description: Seeds irregularly ovoid, globose or isodiametric, 4.5--10 mm diam
vegetative_reproduction_description: The seeds are usually sterile, and reproduction is mostly vegetative by means of proliferating fruit (Backeberg 1958, Walters et al. 2015)
habitat_description: In South Australia, Austrocylindropuntia subulata is naturalised mainly in inland semi-arid and arid areas, as well as near the coast. At Bowman Park near Crystal Brook the plants grow on creek banks among Eucalyptus camaldulensis. In Victoria, Austrocylindropuntia subulata is adventive along a degraded roadside at Birdwoodton (near Mildura), apparently established from a nearby garden.
distribution_description: Probably native to the Andes of Peru, but widely distributed elsewhere such as Argentina and Bolivia (Anderson 2001). Austrocylindropuntia subulata is only known to be naturalised in South Australia and is adventive in Victoria, but the species is present in cultivation in Western Australia and New South Wales (Chinnock 2015). Austrocylindropuntia subulata has been commonly cultivated for decades in Queensland (no naturalised records) and is on an elimination list by Biosecurity Queensland (Paul I. Forster, pers. comm., 16 June 2025).
notes: The seeds are usually sterile, and reproduction is mostly vegetative by means of proliferating fruit (Backeberg 1958, Walters et al. 2015). In Kenya the species has been recorded as invasive, forming dense, impenetrable stands, often around abandoned homesteads (Walters et. al. 2011). In the eastern part of the Iberian Peninsula in Spain near Valencia it is regarded as being the most invasive species of Austrocylindropuntia and Cylindropuntia (Laguna et al. 2013).
