pollination_description: Fruit production in Cereus uruguayanus is dependent on cross-pollination between different individuals (Silva & Sazima 1995)
dispersal_description: Hosking et al. (1988) noted that most of the cacti that are serious weeds in Australia are presumed to have their fruit (and hence seeds) dispersed by birds and mammals
habitat_description: Forster and Schmeider (2000) reported that Cereus uruguayanus is naturalised in several populations in western Queensland on heavy clay soils in natural and disturbed woodland dominated by Acacia harpophylla and Casuarina pauper, with an estimated 3200 individuals over 6 hectares at one of the sites near Glenmorgan, predominantly in clumps of Acacia harpophylla. At Goombungee in southeastern Queensland it is naturalised on a sandstone ridge in woodland dominated by Eucalyptus crebra and Corymbia citriodora. Near Chinchilla in southeastern Queensland it has been collected in woodland dominated by Eucalyptus populnea and Allocasuarina luehmannii. At Thallon in southern-central Queensland it is a weed in Eucalyptus microtheca woodland, on cracking clay soil. There is also a collection from Townsville, where collected from the side of a granitic hill, in disturbed woodland. Near Grawin in northern New South Wales it is a weed in Eucalyptus populnea subsp. bimbil and Callitris sp. woodland, on red sand. Near Dubbo it is a roadside weed, on red alluvial soil. West of Gunnedah it is a weed in Eucalyptus woodland with Geijera parviflora and Dodonaea viscosa subsp. angustifolia and with many herbs including Austrostipa sp., Aristida ramosa, Atriplex semibaccata, on red brown loam.
distribution_description: Indigenous to southern Brazil, through Uruguay and to Argentina (Taylor & Zappi 2006). Naturalised in Queensland and New South Wales. There is a single collection (Chinnock 10104) from South Australia, but the species is not considered to be established in that State.
notes: Fasciation and monstrosity of the stem has frequently been observed in the naturalised populations of Cereus uruguayanus in Australia (Forster & Schmeider 2000). Fruit production in Cereus uruguayanus is dependent on cross-pollination between different individuals (Silva & Sazima 1995). Hosking et al. (1988) noted that most of the cacti that are serious weeds in Australia are presumed to have their fruit (and hence seeds) dispersed by birds and mammals.

This entity has often been referred to as forma monstruosa (e.g. National Herbarium of New South Wales, accessed June 2020). Except for a few populations in Western Australia, flowers and fruits are not produced (Chinnock 2015), and reproduction is vegetative by means of fragmentation. In southern Africa, flood waters are one of the ways that dislodged stem-segments are dispersed (Walters et al. 2011).

It is an environmental weed, invading semi-arid grasslands and dry open woodland such as Callitris glaucophylla woodland, Eucalyptus populnea and Eremophila mitchellii woodland, in northern New South Wales, and Acacia cambagei scrub in Queensland, as well a riparian zones. It also invades agricultural areas and rangelands.

habitat_description: An environmental weed, common in Eucalyptus populnea woodlands and open areas around Lightning Ridge in New South Wales. distribution_description: Cylindropuntia kleinia is known from a single collection each from Western Australia, South Australia and Victoria, but it is moderately common around the Lightning Ridge and Grawin areas in New South Wales. In South Australia it was collected at Barmera in 1980, and is now presumed extinct. The Victorian specimen was collected in 2006, but this population has apparently been destroyed. The incursion in Western Australia was discovered in 2014. The species is native to Northern Mexico, Texas and New Mexico.
notes: Cylindropuntia kleiniae is most likely to be confused with C. leptocaulis, the latter species has stem segments 3--5 mm diam. without obvious tubercles except at apex and when dry, yellow flowers, and red fruits (Chinnock 2015).

In Mitiamo Mineral and Stone Production Reserve, central-northern Victoria, found growing among boulders, in sandy/gravely soil, with a mixture of native vegetation (e.g. Callitris, Acacia, native grasses) and introduced vegetation.

notes: Cylindropuntia leptocaulis is most likely to be confused with C. kleiniae, the latter species has stem segments of 6--12 mm diam. with obvious tubercles, red to magenta flowers, and yellowish orange to brownish orange fruits (Chinnock 2015).

habitat_description: In Australia, Cylindropuntia pallida is predominantly naturalised in the subarid and arid inland regions. It is often associated with homesteads, mining areas, tip sites, but is also an environmental weed. It occurs in a variety of habitats including Eucalyptus woodlands, alluvial floodplains, shrublands and rocky outcrops. It grows on most soil types (NSW WeedWise).
distribution_description: Naturalised in all States except Australian Capital Territory and Tasmania. Native to Mexico (Anderson, 2001).
notes: Cylindropuntia pallida appears to have spread relatively recently, with most records being post 2000 (Chinnock 2015). It is spread vegetatively by segments or fruits which root where they contact the ground. The segments are easily detached, and are can dispersed by flood waters (Walters et al. 2011).

habitat_description: In Australia, Cylindropuntia prolifera is predominantly naturalised in the subarid and arid inland regions. It is often an environmental weed. In Western Australia it was collected from a private property, where growing with Acacia sp. It is relatively widespread in South Australia, and has been collected from gibber desert where growing in association with chenopods and Senna sp., as well as from mallee sites, and Acacia pendula and bluebush association. In Queensland it has been collected from a dry creek bed in Acacia cambagei scrub, and semi-arid/arid grassland. At Lightning Ridge in New South Wales it is a weed in Eucalyptus populnea subsp. bimbil woodland, on red sandy soil, woodland with small shrubs including Geijera parviflora, and a ground layer with many native herbs and grasses. On Nine Mile Station near Broken Hill it is a weed in subarid shrubland on with Atriplex nummularia, Eremophila sturtii, Dodonaea sp. and Pittosporum angustifolium.
distribution_description: Naturalised in Western Australia, South Australia, Queensland and New South Wales. Native to California, Baja California and Mexico (Anderson 2001).
notes: Pinkava (2003) considered Cylindropuntia prolifera to be a hybrid between C. alcahes (F.A.C.Weber) F.M.Knuth and C. cholla (F.A.C.Weber) F.M.Knuth, two Mexican species (not naturalised/present in Australia).

habitat_description: In Australia, Cylindropuntia spinosior is predominantly naturalised in the subarid and arid inland regions, often an environmental weed. It can be an aggressive weed, forming extensive impenetrable stands (Sheehan & Potter 2017). In South Australia it has been collected from In grazed areas, and around mining ruins, and old homesteads. In Queensland it has been collected from around homesteads, stations, rubbish dumps, mulga shrubland, Acacia cambagei shrubland, rocky hillsides with Spinifex sp. and Ghost Gum. Near Lightning Ridge in New South Wales it has been collected from Eucalyptus populnea subsp. bimbil woodland with Geijera parviflora, Eremophila mitchellii and Senna. Near White Cliffs it grows on hillslopes on clay soil, with Maireana pyramidata. In VIctoria it is known from a single collection from near Mildura, where growing along a road in Mairena shrubland with scattered mallee and other cactus species.
distribution_description: Naturalised in South Australia, Queensland, New South Wales and Victoria. Native to Arizona and New Mexico, and northern Mexico (Anderson 2001).
notes: Baker et al. (2018) reduced Cylindropuntia spinosior to a var. of C. imbricata, subsequently elevating it to a subspecies (Baker 2019). Baker et al. (2018, 2019) argued that the placement of Cylindropuntia spinosior within C. imbricata resulted, in part, from recent DNA analyses. Pending a comprehensive morphological and molecular study of these taxa, C. spinosior is here retained at specific rank.

habitat_description: In Australia, Cylindropuntia tunicata is predominantly naturalised in the subarid and arid inland regions, often an environmental weed. In Western Australia it is known only from around Coolgardie where growing on vacant land, and in mallee. In South Australia it has been collected from flats above a creek in Eucalyptus largiflorens woodland on compacted brown loams, where growing with Atriplex lindleyi, Enchylaena tomentosa, Sclerolaena sp. and Mesembryanthemum nodiflorum. In Queensland it has been collected from woodland dominated by Acacia harpophylla, A. salicina, Geijera parviflora and Lysiphyllum, on heavy clay soil. In New South Wales, it is found in the North Western Plains area, around the Grawin opal fields, where naturalised in Eucalyptus populnea subsp. bimbil woodland, on red sand. In Victoria it is grows in mixed mallee woodland, with chenopod understorey.
distribution_description: Naturalised in Western Australia, South Australia, Queensland, New South Wales and Victoria. Native to the Chihuahuan Desert in northern Mexico and Texas. It also occurs in Ecuador and Chile, where presumably introduced (Anderson 2001).

It can form extensive, impenetrable stands to the exclusion of native herbs and shrubs, impede the movement of native fauna and stock, and provide habitat for pest species such as rabbits (Sheehan & Potter 2017).

distribution_description: Benson (1982) considered Opuntia dillenii to be indigenous on the east coast of Mexico to northern South America, the West Indies and Bermuda. Anderson (2001) cites the distribution as southeastern U.S.A, the Caribbean, Mexico, Central America and Ecuador. The plants in Ecuador have been placed in Opuntia melanosperma Svenson by some authors, which is usually considered as a taxonomic synonym of O. dillenii (Menkins 2022b). Menkins notes that populations from the Gulf coast and offshore islands of the United States may be referable to O. bentonii Griffiths (often treated as a synonym O. stricta) and O. anahuacensis Griffiths (placed by Benson (1982) in O. stricta var. dillenii and by Anderson (2001) in O. dillenii). The current Australian Plant Census distribution indicates that the species is sparingly established in Queensland, and naturalised in New South Wales. Menkins (2022b) notes that the species is widespread and common throughout Australia but does not list the States. Menkins (pers. comm., March 2022) has found O. stricta to generally be more coastal and confined to southern states, and O. dillenii the most widespread, but there are examples of overlapping distribution.

habitat_description: In Australia, Opuntia elatior is predominantly naturalised in the subarid and arid inland regions, but also occurs in temperate regions such as in Melbourne. In Western Australia it has been collected from mulga woodland, on stony red loam along a drainage line, and along streams. In the Northern Territory it has been collected from the base of a rocky sandstone hill. The species is more widespread in South Australia, and has been collected from a dune on a pastoral station near a homestead, rocky outcrops, and near homesteads. In Queensland it is known from a single collection from a heavily grazed paddock, on cracking black clay, on the Condamine flood plain. In New South Wales it has been collected from open forest, and in Victoria, known at a single site on a road cutting at Studley Park in Melbourne, where evidently established from cultivated plants above road cutting.
distribution_description: Sporadically naturalised predominantly through inland Australia south from Alice Springs, but extending south to Melbourne. Present in Western Australia, Northern Territory, South Australia, Queensland, New South Wales and Victoria. The Victorian occurrence is not substantiated by herbarium specimens, however, plants were observed at Studley Park (Kew) in 1995, by Val Stajsic and G.W. Carr. The natural distribution of Opuntia elatior is uncertain. Hunt et al. (2006) cite the Lesser Antilles, Netherlands Antilles, Colombia, Costa Rica, Panama and Venezuela. The species has been widely distributed by humans (Anderson 2001). It is likely to be native to Colombia and Venezuela, but records from Panama and Costa Rica are uncertain, and records from the Caribbean islands may be more recent introductions (Pasiecznik 2015). Opuntia bergeriana, a possible synonym of O. elatior but recognised by some authors (e.g. Innes & Glass 1991), is not known to occur in the wild naturally, but is naturalised in parts of the French and Italian Riviera (Hunt et al. 2006). Hunt et al. (2006) comment that although Opuntia elatior is supposedly a well-known and widespread species, no illustrations of 'typical' O. elatior were available for their publication. They also suggest that it might be masquerading under one or more names provisionally accepted for illustrations (in volume 2 of their publication) for O. pittieri, O. sanguinea, O. schumannii and O. soederstromiana. It's also possible that there is more than one species masquerading under the name Opuntia elatior in Australia.

notes: Cultivation and selection since prehistoric times in tropical America have resulted in many horticultural variants. Several genotypes have been introduced into Australia. Most commonly grown is a spineless cultivar. Some naturalised populations belong to the spiny variant previously known as O. megacantha. Opuntia amyclea Tenore reported from ‘Glenmore’ near Rockhampton last century, and plants known as Joconoxtle also from central Queensland, probably represent other spiny variants. Here also may belong O. pachona Griffiths, recorded from Pallamallawa, New South Wales, in 1923 (Mann 1970: 30). Opuntia ficus-indica is grown commercially in parts of Australia (e.g. South Australia, Victoria), and it is been excluded from noxious weeds lists in New South Wales since 1978, and has never been declared in Victoria. Harvey (2009) mentions that the dispersal of O. ficus-indica by birds has never been recorded in Australia. Contrary to this claim, the species is indeed dispersed by birds such as Little Ravens at some sites, (e.g. Bacchus Marsh, Victoria) where birds were actively observed feeding on the fruit from a commercial crop, with young plants established on the slopes above the farm (V. Stajsic, pers. observ.). Indeed, Parsons (1992) mentions that birds, foxes and other animals disperse the seed of Opuntia robusta, which also has edible fruit, and there's no reason why that would not be the case in O. ficus-indica.

distribution_description: Possibly the most widely distributed species of Opuntia in Australia, but that is now unclear given the work by Menkins (2022b). Believed to be indigenous to the southeastern U.S.A., eastern Mexico and Cuba (Anderson 2001; Hunt et al. 2006).
notes: Wild native populations show morphological intergradation in habit and spininess. Several genotypes appear to have been introduced into Australia (Murray 1982), some of which have been interpreted as distinct species. Opuntia stricta is widely naturalised in all Australian mainland States. From garden escapes of the mid-1800s, by the mid-1920s Opuntia stricta had infested c. 24 million hectares of central and southern Queensland and northern New South Wales. The biological control of Prickly Pear, largely by the introduction of the Phycitid moth Cactoblastis cactorum Berg from Argentina, is one of the most spectacular successes of economic entomology, and is documented by Dodd (1940), Mann (1970) and Osmond and Munro (1981). Natural hybrids with Opuntia humifusa occur in southeastern U.S.A. Putative hybrids have been observed in the Hunter Valley, New South Wales, where both species are naturalised.

Mueller s.n., without date, but possibly from the 1860s (MEL1620318A) is labelled ‘Moreton’s Bay, spontaneous’, the first record of the species becoming naturalised in Australia (Telford 1984).

common_name: Night-blooming Cereus, Queen of the Night, Moonlight Cactus, Dragon Fruit, Night-blooming Cactus, White-fleshed Pitahaya.

habitat_description: In Australia, Selenicereus undatus is naturalised predominantly in coastal and near-coastal areas of Queensland, and far northeastern New South Wales. It is an environmental weed of open woodlands, dry rainforest, vine forest, riparian areas and coastal vegetation. It also persists in old gardens, and near refuse tips.
distribution_description: Origin uncertain because of its long history in cultivation. Probably indigenous to tropical America (Hunt et al. 2011), perhaps Mexico and Central America (Taylor & Zappi 2004). In Australia, naturalised predominantly in near-coastal southeastern Queensland, with outliers at Somerset Homestead ruins, Somerset, at the tip of Cape York Peninsula, and Townsville. Also naturalised in far northeastern New South Wales.

habit_description: Tree to 25 m high
leaf_description: Leaves | petiole 1.2--2.5 cm long | lamina elliptic, oblong or narrowly ovate, usually 8--20 cm long, 3--10 cm wide, decurrent or attenuate at base, acuminate, glabrous, usually with 7--15 pairs of secondary veins

habitat_description: Grows in complex mesophyll vine forest.
distribution_description: Occurs in northeastern Queensland from Oliver Creek to Mackenzie Creek, N of Daintree and also Russell River and Harvey Creek.
notes: The seeds contain toxins (Everist 1981, Duke et al. 1995, Gordon & Reddell 2004, McKenzie 2012). Discovered in 1902 and described in 1912 by German botanist Ludwig Diels as Calycanthus australiensis, the species was rediscovered in the Daintree in the early 1970s when cattle were poisoned and died after ingesting the seeds. In 1972 Stanley Blake reassigned the species to the genus Idiospermum its own family Idiospermaceae.

distribution_description: S.A. (naturalised), N.S.W. (naturalised), Vic. (naturalised), Tas. (sparingly naturalised). Native to tropical and southern Africa.

notes: The habit varies according to severity or otherwise of the substrate, being more stunted and caespitose in exposed clefts in rocks.

habitat_description: Grows in rainforest. A shrub in depauperate rainforest thickets to a canopy tree in monsoon rainforest. According to Zich et al. (2020), grows in drier, more seasonal rainforest often associated with Kauri Pine (Agathis robusta).
distribution_description: Occurs in coastal districts and up to 100 km inland, from Cape York Peninsula, Queensland, S to the Manning River, New South Wales; also in the Philippines, New Guinea and the Solomon Islands.

notes: See Shepherd (2004: 34) and McKenzie (2012: 467--469) for details on toxicity and impacts of use.

In Victoria recorded as weakly naturalised near Red Cliffs in the far northwest, and Myrtleford in the northeast (Walsh 2015). There are also records from southeastern South Australia.

distribution_description: One subspecies, Celtis conferta subsp. amblyphylla (F.Muell.) P.S.Green, is endemic to Lord Howe Island. The other, Celtis conferta Planch. subsp. conferta, is confined to New Caledonia.

ecology_description: Bird dispersed seeds (Department of Environment and Climate Change (NSW) 2007: 129).

In Victoria, weakly naturalised on Yarra River flats near Heidelberg (Walsh 2015). In the Australian Capital Territory it has been recorded from bushland with weeds in a creek bed at Mount Pleasant.

ecology_description: Food plant for the larval stages of the Common Aeroplane and Tailed Emperor butterflies (Common & Waterhouse 1981, per Zich et al. 2020). Fruit eaten by Pied Imperial-pigeons and Great Bowerbirds (Cooper & Cooper 2004: 546).
habitat_description: Grows in a wide range of soil types (basaltic, granitic, calcareous, sandy, humus-rich) and in a wide range of habitats (sandy beaches, beach forest, littoral rainforest, vine thickets/forest, monsoon forest, drier, more seasonal rainforest, sclerophyll forest) being somewhat mesophytic in wetter habitats and xerophytic in drier habitats.
distribution_description: Occurs in northeastern Northern Territory (E of Rosie Creek area, including near off-shore islands (e.g. Pellow Islands) in the Gulf of Carpentaria) and from Cape York, Queensland, south to coastal central New South Wales; also on Norfolk Island and in Melanesia, Polynesia and Malesia.
seedling_description: This species has folded cotyledons.
notes: A collection made on Sweers Island, 1901, J.F. Bailey (BRI) claims to be a collection from the 'Investigator Tree'. D.J. Mabberley, Jupiter Botanicus 103 (1985) reported that Matthew Flinders 'left "the name of 'H.M.S. Investigator', with the date 1802" carved on a tree, which, with "heaps of broken bottles", was all that remained in 1880 of the thriving township of Carnarvon which grew up ... The tree blew down in 1887 bearing thirteen ships' inscriptions including that of the Beagle (1841).' If the Bailey collection is authentic then the tree must have persisted. For treatment of Celtis paniculata on Norfolk Island where it is an occasional but widespread tree see Green (1994: 59).

common_name: Celtis, Gulyindji [Bardi Tribe of the Kimberley], Angarrakaba [Groote Eylandt], Malaiino, Kaju Lulu.

habitat_description: Grows in a wide range of habitats and in a wide range of soil types, including basalt, quartzite, sandstone, limestone, coastal sand and black peaty soil. Habitats include open sclerophyll forest, rainforest, monsoon forest, vine forest and coastal dunes.
distribution_description: Occurs in the Kimberley, Western Australis, in northern Northern Territory and from Cape York Peninsula south to Broad Sound, Queensland. Also occurs in tropical Africa, through India, southeast Asia and Malesia to the Solomon Islands.
seedling_description: Celtis philippensis has flat cotyledons.
notes: The species is markedly xerophytic in drier habitats. In Western Australis and adjacent Northern Territory, the leaves are the smallest, apiculate, with more-persistent indumentum and often with toothed margins. In Australia the trees do not reach the sizes reported by E. Soepadmo in Flora Malesiana ser. 1, 8: 62 (1977).

notes: Resembles Cinnamomum iners Reinw. ex Blume in its 3-veined leaf, but can easily be distinguished by its serrulate leaf margin. The bark is distinctively mottled inside. The wood smells foetid due to the presence of skatole, and is said to drive away evil spirits.

distribution_description: Indigenous in Europe and Western Asia N of 32°; in Australia cultivated in cooler areas of South Australia, New South Wales and Tasmania, but few collections outside cultivation. Occasionally naturalised with records from Western Australia, South Australia, New South Wales, Victoria and Tasmania.

notes: May have medicinal properties; it may also be poisonous (Zich et al. 2020).

distribution_description: The native range is thought to be throughout Europe except in the extreme north but Stellaria media is currently found on every continent, absent only from the Polar Regions and very dry areas. In Australia it occurs in the north from Bundaberg, Queensland, along the east coast and Great Dividing Range through New South Wales to the Victorian coast and mountains, along the Murray floodplain and west to South Australia from Adelaide and surrounding ranges as far west as Port Lincoln. It also occurs on Norfolk and Lord Howe Islands, in eastern Tasmania, the Bass Strait Islands and on Macquarie Island. There are a few records for the Northern Territory from Alice Springs, and in Western Australia from coastal areas from Albany to just north of Perth. A single specimen is known from Kununurra in northern Western Australia. There are also scattered occurrences outside these areas in gardens. It is an important economic weed of crops.

distribution_description: The native range of Stellaria pallida extends throughout most of central to western and southern Europe. It has also spread as a weed into the Americas and Asia. Found at scattered localities within New South Wales, along the Great Dividing Range from Tenterfield to Canberra, with one collection inland at Broken Hill. It also occurs along the Murray River drainage system in New South Wales and Victoria. It is found in most areas of Victoria except alpine areas as well as throughout coastal and coastal ranges of South Australia including Kangaroo Island; the northern most collections extend into the Flinders Ranges and the western most collection is at Fowlers Bay near Ceduna. This species is uncommon in Tasmania, being mainly found on offshore islands and in coastal regions but occasionally further inland. It is also uncommon in Western Australia with coastal collections from Rottnest Island and Busselton in the west, Bremer Bay in the south and Cocklebiddy in the east near the South Australian border.
notes: This weed probably has a wider distribution in Australia than listed here but is often overlooked or misidentified as Stellaria media. From examining the herbarium collections it appears S. pallida is a relatively recent introduction to Australia. There are very few collections prior to the 1950s with the earliest collection recorded in 1905 at Tallandoon in Victoria, whereas S. media had been recorded from most states by the mid-1800s. Also see notes under S. media.
